[h1]Montre-moi où tu vis, je devinerai qui tu es[/h1]

[h1]En résumé[/h1]
[list]
    [*] Un jeu très qualitatif du point de vue graphique et musical
    [*] Une expérience narrative originale via le process de déballer et ranger
    [*] Mais le sentiment qu'il est trop court et inabouti (voir plus bas)
[/list]
_______________

[h1]Plus en détails[/h1]
_______________

Vous avez envie de découvrir une histoire sans texte, où vos yeux et déductions remplaceront les mots ? Cette narration presque muette, mais musicale, est au croisement entre jeu de détente, d'album photo, de décoration et de rangement.


[h1]Un jeu de rangement, mais détente[/h1]
Le gameplay est simple : [b]déballer des cartons et ranger[/b]. Encore, encore et encore. Difficile d'imaginer que ce soit un jeu détente ? Et pourtant...
Je vous rassure, pas besoin d'être Marie Kondo pour l'apprécier (au contraire si vous êtes organisé, les cartons assez chaotiques vont plutôt vous laisser perplexe, voire vous agacer un tantinet).

Mais pour une raison obscure, [b]les graphismes mignons et l'ambiance relax[/b] vous font oublier que vous êtes en train de faire des corvées que vous détesteriez faire dans la vraie vie. Et qu'en plus, vous avez payé pour ça.

Unpacking est un jeu [b]chill, en quelque sorte méditatif[/b], qui ne posera aucune difficulté particulière - si ce n'est une légère impression de Tetris dans certains petits espaces.
Mais promis, vous vous en sortirez, et chaque pièce/logement terminé procure un sentiment de satisfaction indescriptible. Que vous pouvez en plus immortaliser en photo, avec filtres et stickers. C'est pas beau la vie ?


[h1]Une narration presque muette[/h1]
Mais on ne peut pas résumer Unpacking à l'action de ranger. Non, [b]Unpacking a une âme[/b], un concept narratif qui le rend si spécial.

Le jeu ne vous dira rien, hormis une petite ligne en fin de chapitre, qui commente la photo (pour toutes les découvrir, rouvrez le logement et changez de pièce, car ça change selon la pièce). Mais ce ne sont pas des révélations, juste des choses que vous aurez déjà comprises.

La particularité de cette histoire, c'est que vous êtes [b]à la fois le spectateur et le protagoniste[/b]. Protagoniste, car c'est vous qui déballez et placez les affaires du perso. Mais spectateur de sa vie, car vous ne savez rien de lui et avez tout à découvrir (je ne ferai aucun spoil).

Autrement dit, vous êtes dans sa vie au moment d'emménager, mais absent le reste du temps. Et c'est ça qui nous intéresse : qui est ce perso ? Quel âge a-t-il, qu'est-ce qu'il aime, qu'est-ce qu'il devient ? Quels tournants sa vie a-t-elle pris depuis la dernière fois ? Les endroits et les cartons regorgent d'indices pour le découvrir. C'est comme un livre que vous ne lirez pas, ou un film mis en pause sur le décor, où c'est [b]à vous de chercher, observer, comprendre[/b].

Et c'est ça qui nous tient en haleine, qui fait que malgré la répétition, on ne se lasse jamais de déballer et ranger - et demanderait à le faire encore des heures.


[h1]Un peu court et inabouti[/h1]
Et c'est là qu'on arrive au point faible de ce jeu : sa durée (entre 3 et 8h selon votre efficacité et vos tocs de rangement, et selon votre plaisir à traîner sur les détails).

Comme tout le monde, je pourrais dire "[b][i]gneugneu le jeu est trop court pour son prix[/i][/b]". Et c'est vrai, mais ça va au-delà.

Vous l'avez compris, dans Unpacking on est pris par l'histoire. On consacre littéralement tout notre temps à bichonner une personne via ses lieux de vie, à être content ou triste pour elle en fonction de ce qui lui arrive, et à la voir grandir / vieillir. On se donne du mal, on [b]veut[/b] connaître l'étape suivante. Perso pour 20€, je m'attends à [b]suivre le perso assez vieux[/b], ou au moins à voir une étape de vie bouclée, quelque chose d'abouti en substance.

C'était pas le cas ici. [b]Le jeu s'arrête assez brutalement[/b], d'un coup vous découvrez que vous étiez au tout dernier chapitre. Il y a une pseudo-image de fin et une (très belle) musique, mais c'est comme si ça s'était arrêté en cours de route, trop jeune, trop tôt. Pourquoi à ce moment-là, on ne sait pas. Le chapitre regorgeait de potentiel et d'indices sur la suite, [b]vous êtes en plein dans vos hypothèses[/b] et pouf, écran de fin. Vous avez passé quelques heures à faire l'histoire dans votre tête ? Maintenant continuez sans les images.

C'est comme ces vieux films français qui n'ont pas de fin, où c'est à vous d'imaginer le reste. Il y a une certaine poésie, mais le réalisateur n'a pas pris la peine d'aller au bout de l'intrigue principale, voire de clore d'autres choses qu'il a initiées en cours de route. Vu la qualité du jeu, je doute que ce soit par flemme, mais je ne comprends pas le choix d'arrêter précisément là. J'aurais bien vu un chapitre de plus pour "boucler la boucle", ou davantage.

A mes yeux [b]le concept n'est pas abouti[/b], et aurait mérité soit de survoler plusieurs personnages, soit d'explorer toutes les étapes d'une vie, soit de couvrir une période plus définie et avec plus de profondeur.

Par ailleurs, même la période choisie est peu équilibrée : il y a des gros sauts dans le temps, et à l'inverse d'autres chapitres très rapprochés, sans pouvoir déduire nettement un axe ou un parti-pris.


[h1]Pour conclure[/h1]
Unpacking est un jeu assez qualitatif, qui mérite les louages que vous pouvez lire et entendre à son sujet. Mais à mes yeux, le jeu n'est pas allé au bout de son concept et de son potentiel. La durée, la fin un peu brutale et l'absence d'enjeu bien défini nous laissent sur notre faim.

En définitive la période jouée aura manqué d'accomplissement et de profondeur, il aurait fallu la prolonger ou au moins la boucler.

Pour cette raison je le recommande oui, mais en promo.

I  went into *Unpacking* thinking it would just be a nice, relaxing little game where you put things away, but it ended up being surprisingly nostalgic and emotional.

You follow the girl through different stages of her life, and you learn about her through all the little things she owns. I kept recognising things from my own childhood and thinking, “I had one of those!” 😂

Seeing her grow up, move house, change interests and eventually make a home of her own was honestly lovely. It brought back so many memories of growing up myself.

It's simple, cosy and incredibly satisfying to play. I really didn't expect a game about unpacking boxes to make me feel so nostalgic, but here we are. 😂📦❤️

[h1] Paz y sosiego: [/h1]
En lo que respecta a ser algo tan profundamente básico, no significa que sea malo.
Los juegos no son incitaciones a la violencia. Aportan tranquilidad mental y relajación, ya sea por tu dura jornada laboral como por cualquier otro motivo. Te ayudan a desconectar de lo que te rodea, lo cual hay muchas formas de ello.
Unpacking, lo dice claramente, desempaquetar tu equipaje, por mudanza o lo que sea.
Y la ironía (por así decirlo), es que desempaquetando cosas por mudanzas en el ámbito real, puede ocasionarte estrés; aquí en el juego te ocasiona serenidad.
Este juego te ofrece, solamente, distracción, tranquilidad y entretenimiento.
Hasta el sistema de logros, ya sea algo corto, es entretenido.
Es de corta duración, sí, pero es un juego hecho para que lo juegues cuando necesites realmente desconectar de todo, o estés enfermo/a. Ayuda a distraerte y sosegarte mentalmente.

Unpacking – это супер уютная, забавная, маленькая «дзен-игра». Чистая, яркая пиксельная графика и ностальгический 8-битный саундтрек соответствут простой, но в то же время удивительно глубокой идее формирования повествования посредством переезда и распаковки коробок. Там нет очков, рекордов, ограничений по времени или чего-то еще. Есть небольшая скрытая история из жизни этого человека, которую было интересно узнать, когда я распаковывала вещи. 

Красота этой игры в тонкости, с которой она передает очень важное послание. Вы будете вместе с главной героиней буквально переживать ее переход во взрослую жизнь. Вы заметите маленькие изменения, которые происходят с ее образом жизни каждый год. Вы заметите, что некоторые предметы остались позади и что у персонажа появились новые дополнения к серии книг например. 

Единственное что меня расстроило, так это ограничение при выборе постановки предметов. Это связано с тем, что игра не дает возможность поместить определенные объекты для прохождения уровня. Обычно размещение относительно свободное и интуитивно понятное, но иногда то место, где я хотела разместить элемент, и то место, где его хотели разместить разработчики, не совпадали. 

Еще один не минус, а больше расстраивающий меня факт — невозможность вращать комнату. Это имеет смысл, поскольку игра нарисована в пиксельной графике, но все же хотелось бы иметь возможность покрутить комнату и посмотреть на нее с разных ракурсов. 

Саундтрек в игре приятный и расслабляющий. 

Советую.

Unpacking not just a box, but a life.
通过一次又一次的unpacking来窥探一段段经历与人生，从小小的毛绒玩具和摆件之间读出悲欢离合。新奇而简单的叙事方式，轻华容道式的游戏体验，辅以细节上惹人会心一笑的小小互动，让两三个小时的游戏流程非常轻松舒缓。
适合安静地独自游玩。
基本不会存在卡关问题，但也有时会因为生活文化差异搞不懂一些物件的用途，耐心多试几次就能得答案。
对于绝大多数人来说，搬家的次数在一生中大概屈指可数。每一次从零开始，让行李填满光秃秃的屋子时，心里都充满了对接下来一段崭新生活的期待吧。陪伴我们留下来的东西除非必要，否则都是如此宝贵，承载了过去的时光，从上一段生活中传承下来。
打开箱子，为见证了过去的老伙伴找一个新的安身之所吧，然后向前看，因为我们视线所及的地方，正是一段崭新的人生。

A simple vista, parece un juego chill de abrir cajas de cartón, sacar tus cosas y colocarlas en los estantes con una música tranquila de fondo. 

Pero si te paras a mirarlo con un poco de atención, te das cuenta de que te está contando algo mucho más grande. Te está hablando de la vida misma, del paso del tiempo y de cómo cambiamos sin poder hacer nada para frenarlo.

El juego no usa palabras, no las necesita. Te cuenta la historia de una persona a través de los objetos que decide llevarse consigo en cada mudanza. Y ahí es donde te da el golpe de realidad, porque te hace pensar en tu propia maleta.

Las cosas que se quedan por el camino.

Jugarlo te hace darte cuenta de cosas que todos vivimos al hacernos mayores:

Lo que ya no cabe: Notas cómo juguetes o recuerdos que a los 18 años eran tu mundo entero, a los 25 ya no tienen sentido y se quedan guardados al fondo de un armario. Tu mente cambia, tus prioridades cambian, y tus cosas también.

Forzarnos a encajar: Hay momentos en los que se ve perfectamente cómo intentamos encogernos para caber en la vida de otra persona, guardando lo nuestro donde no moleste porque no nos dan nuestro sitio. Y cómo, tarde o temprano, toca empaquetar de nuevo y marcharse.

Avanzar sin frenos: Al final, no tienes el control de lo que pasa fuera. El tiempo no se para. Las etapas se cierran, las personas se van y el camión de la mudanza arranca quieras o no. Solo te queda decidir qué te quedas y qué dejas atrás en la acera para poder seguir adelante.

En resumen:
Este juego es un espejo. Te enseña que hacernos mayores va exactamente de eso: de ir abriendo cajas, aprender a soltar lo que ya no nos suma, quedarnos con lo que de verdad importa y aceptar que la vida es un constante cambio. Una auténtica joya que te deja pensando en tus propias mudanzas mucho después de haber apagado la pantalla.

[/spoiler] (Minor spoiler.) It goes on from there. The next residence may, perhaps, give you a clue about what's to come after that, but I won't spoil it.  This game is, by the way, very LGBTQ+ positive, which is a plus in my book. :)

Unpacking is a really cute game where you're unpacking moving boxes as you move into new homes from childhood to adulthood. I was expecting a relaxing game to help me unwind and feel satisfied after putting every item in their place. I was not expecting the interesting story-telling that comes from seeing what the character owns, what things they've kept around, and what things they've gotten rid of. I think this story-telling is so creative because you get a sense of who this character is and what's happening in their life without a single line of dialogue or any cutscenes.

While I really appreciate this game, I think this price point is a bit high for the amount of gameplay and levels the game has to offer. I got the game half-price and played the game twice over (once the regular way with each item in their spot to get gold stars, and once in the "secret" way to get all dark stars), and I think even at that discounted price the game should've been longer. They could've included a few more homes, or having a completely different character and their storyline, which I think could be really interesting since one of my favourite aspects of this game is the creative storytelling.

Overall, I recommend checking out the game but only if it's on sale.

Unpacking by Witch Beam is made by an indie developer based in Brisbane, Australia

The player follows an unknown girl's partial journey through life. It begins when she first leaves home and we are greeted with boxes in each room of a small apartment. The story is not narrated, but well told through the different lodgings and belongings we have to put away from boxes. It definitely gives the player emotional responses, even without words, as the journey unfolds. With each new abode, new items will be added, and some will be left behind.

In it's essence, it is a puzzle game. Most items have limited possibilities of where they can be placed. If an item is not placed in one of its correct possible spots, the player is alerted and the item is outlined in red.

It can sometimes be quite a task to find a place for an item in an already crowded placement area. Thankfully the player can put items on the floor (or some other positions) in order to rearrange and make space for the item in crowded spots.

Pros:
* A very well made game which made it a joy to play
* An emotional journey, zen like, without words
* Mid level saving allowing the play at your own pace
* Easily accessible by players of all skill levels 
* Lovely music and graphics
* Possible replay value to get achievements (25 in total) when not using a guide
* Trading Cards

Cons:
* A little on the pricey side for a roughly 4 hour game
* A lot of the achievements will require revealing achievement spoilers or using a guide

Final Thoughts:
Even with the high price tag, it proved to be a very enjoyable, worthwhile and memorable journey. The quality in all aspects of the game makes it shine and a joy to play. Definitely an easy recommendation.

Rating : 8/10 (would be more except it is a little short)

1. The big idea here is to tell a story entirely through objects, without any writing. But paradoxically, in order to achieve that I think the game actually needs more writing? I don't mean narrative, obviously, but rather item descriptions: what are the objects? Where are they from? What are they used for? What are the titles of the books and the names of the videogames?

2. On a purely practical level, this small change would solve one of the biggest annoyances of this game, which is the one or two objects that you just don't recognize from their vague pixel art, so after finishing the rest of the level you end up randomly trying to place them everywhere because you have no idea where they're supposed to go. The whiteboard seems to be a particular problem for a lot of people, so wouldn't an item description be nice? A blurb that says "Magnetic Whiteboard" when you click, maybe a little description of what's written on the whiteboard? I feel like even just that would add so much depth to the game.

3. I know this sounds like a small nitpick, but I don't think it's a coincidence that a lot of reviews here say they quite liked the game but that it just wasn't worth the money they spent. That was my experience as well, and I really think it's because the whole experience just feels so insubstantial. There's no texture to the objects, so they all feel bland and featureless. Book with green spine, book with blue spine, you forget about most of these objects as soon as you place them because there's nothing there to hold onto.

Throughout the game, all you do is unpack. You never see or hear any characters. It's just taking stuff out of boxes. And yet somehow, it became one of my favorite games of the year. There is still very much a story to tell, ways to get to know the characters just by the items you're unpacking and where certain items are meant to be placed. It's such an incredible journey to start unpacking your childhood bedroom, through college, [spoiler] entering a crummy relationship, moving back home, then finding a better partner and starting a family [/spoiler]. Only this game can make me sob with joy through the simple act of taking stuff out of boxes.

Only downside is that while it can be replayed to have a chill time, once you get through it there likely won't be a lot of replayability for some people, so it may not justify the $20 price tag. If you're even slightly interested in this game I highly recommend getting it and experiencing it for yourself, but maybe once it's on sale.

游戏好玩是没得说的，画风清爽，玩法休闲，待整理物品考虑得十分周全，关卡设计得很有个性特点，也有在好好讲故事。
就是想吐槽一点自由度的问题。为啥看起来什么都能放的多层置物架，这也不能放那也不能放？为啥枕头底下能放随身听，游戏机就不能放？以前睡觉前日常打PSP的我实在觉得不合理啊……包括吉他不能放床头柜弹，茶具不能放在茶几上，还有不少地方我都觉得可以把限制放得更宽一点。或者甚至可以出一种任意模式，在通了一关以后就可以随便布置，看看大家能把家收拾得多有想象力或者多欢乐，应该会更有趣一点？
还有有的东西我真的不知道是啥，原谅我思路清奇，让有些关的结束部分变得有点折磨……现在玩到第四关，客厅里掏出来个东西看起来像吸尘器（也许实际上也不是很像），哪都放不了，后来随便乱试放到音箱上就好了，就直接谢天谢地不管了。后来想想可能是能放磁带的录音机，那为什么不能放地上呢？我现在脑海里都还一直在想象把自家吸尘器放到音箱上的场景（虽然家里并没有音箱）。厨房里为什么有一套像化学实验室里面简单制备工具的东西啊？还有一个冰箱贴和两幅小画的大小一样，外观看起来也区别不了，关键是三张东西还能叠在一起……作者你知道我花了多久才突破“这三张东西是同种物品”这个认知吗？说起冰箱贴，那几个星星、爱心什么的冰箱贴，第一次出现的时候我真的不知道它们到底是什么，除了是简单的贴纸或者小玩具之外还能是什么，以及这种天真可爱的简单图案既然不能随便放，那么它们的归属到底在哪？还有第二关那个主色是紫色的鼠标垫——是的，经过两关的思考，我现在确实知道它是鼠标垫了。开始的时候哪哪放不对，我就开始想家里有什么方形的薄片状物体，体重秤也不是，菜板也不是（这么五彩斑斓的菜板已经有点离谱了），是什么现代艺术的画作吗，也不是。后来无意间发现它居然可以放在卧室桌子上，毕竟当时我已经把卧室桌子摆满了，又好一阵倒腾，就挺纳闷的，也不管了。到下一关偶然发现鼠标可以移动到这个薄片上，我才反应过来，这就是个鼠标垫。

不行，整理游戏却对强迫症不友好，玩着玩着就很恼火。
有些东西压根不知道是啥，连个物品名称都没有，卡关了还没有引导（鬼知道要把前男友照片塞柜子里）
定价还很贵，不如去玩a little to the left

I'll start by saying that Unpacking, a game about taking objects out of a box and placing them in a room, wasn't for me. On paper it should've been, so for this review I'll try and explain why I didn't like it and why it seems like I should have, and then come to some kind of conclusion.

Something I spend countless hours doing in Bethesda RPGs is organising my inventory and also storing my items in various containers in the many designated player houses you have in those games. I do this because I generally like order and probably have a little OCD. I also don't like to throw stuff away in games, in case I need it later, and Bethesda RPGs overload you, quite literally, with junk. I also tend to hang onto special weapons and armour, "in case I want to try them out later, or change my look", I say to myself. Or perhaps there'll be a situation where I'll need a particular gun or piece of armour, and because I've got all those items neatly placed in different containers (based on item type), it'll be a simple case of fast travelling back to base and picking them up. 

In reality, I tend to find a few guns that I like and stick with them for the majority of the game, with most special weapons getting some cursory use before being placed into storage. Whilst armour is a little more flexible and situational early on, I'll eventually reach a point where I'll just use the best item, stats wise, for my particular character. Or the one I think looks coolest.

But if you enjoy all this item management then what's the problem? The thing is, I don't enjoy it. It's more like a compulsion; the act of moving items between various locations and containers is actually incredibly tedious, made even more of a chore thanks to Bethesda's cumbersome UIs. The process starts feeling like work and it's about as rewarding, and pointless, as working a 9-5 data entry job. And you get paid to do the data entry. You also get to go back to a real house. Why exactly am I making, and stocking, a house in a video game? I'm never going to go back there years later. If I play the game again I'll restart it and all that unpacking will have been pointless. 

I also tend to hit a moment in these games where I notice I'm doing a lot of item management and at that point I tell myself, "either carry on with the main quest or stop playing the game, because you're wasting your time". This was even the case with my beloved Fallout: New Vegas, but once I forced myself to abandon the busy work I was completely absorbed by the game's world and story.

Perhaps this is why the only survival/crafting game I've ever been into is Subnautica, because the crafting has a purpose and it's tied to the narrative. I like to think there's a reason I'm doing something in a game.

In unpacking you are rearranging the belongings of a fictional person over the course of their life, in the various houses they 'lived' in. As should be apparent from my Bethesda compulsions, I like to arrange things irl, and so the books and nik-naks I own and collect are ordered. There is a satisfaction to this, and a purpose*. There is nothing satisfying about unpacking some digital items that aren't mine, for a faceless avatar, other than the little endorphin hit you get from ordering things. There is also no point to it and so all you're really left with is the compulsion.

I have seen people say that the items you unpack and the various houses you fill up, tell a story; but it's a superficial, paper thin narrative, relying on lots of input and interpretation from the player. There are no notes or voice acting, just stuff to unpack and repack. 

Unpacking is obviously a casual game and has no pretensions of being something more. It's the kind of thing you can play whilst doing something else. For some people that's great, but I often find that if I'm doing two things at once, then one of them is getting far less attention. Unpacking doesn't have the replay value of a lot of those multitask games either. 

So all that rambling has hopefully explained, in far too much detail, why I don't recommend Unpacking. I don't hate it, because it's not offensive and does what it says on the tin. But I'd still rather have left it packed.

*The collecting of ultimately worthless material things and the value we place on them, is a discussion for another time.

Un petit jeu de détente, sans prise de tête, et très plaisant pour passer un bel après-midi ou une soirée cosy, j'ai pour ma part beaucoup aimé "Unpacking" ! 
Le principe du jeu est certes simple, mais il devient rapidement addictif. Je n'ai pas vu le temps passer durant les quelques heures que j'ai consacrées à ce jeu, tant j'étais captivée par celui-ci !

J'ai vraiment apprécié le gameplay, il nous permet de suivre les déménagements d'un endroit à un autre tout en déballant les nombreux cartons et en les plaçant à l'endroit qui nous semble le plus approprié (bien que cela soit parfois un peu limité, nous avons tout de même une certaine liberté de choix). 

Parallèlement, nous découvrons l'histoire d'une femme (dont le prénom peut être personnalisé au début) à travers ses différentes résidences, en commençant par sa chambre d'adolescente chez ses parents, puis dans des logements étudiants durant ses années universitaires, ses premiers appartements en colocation, puis avec son petit ami, sa rupture difficile et son retour chez ses parents pendant un certain temps, jusqu'à la conclusion, où elle parvient à retrouver son indépendance et sa liberté, avec un nouveau logement et une nouvelle partenaire pour fonder une famille.

J'ai trouvé son récit émouvant, à la fois subtil et bien retranscrit. Il n'y a pas de dialogues et le personnage n'apparaît jamais, mais on parvient à saisir aisément sa vie personnelle, ses préférences, ses passions, ce qu'elle aime faire pendant son temps libre, à travers tous ses objets (on retrouve souvent les mêmes, c'était très bien conçu et crédible !) que l'on prend plaisir à déballer et à organiser à notre manière, tout en observant l'usure du temps qui s'est écoulé pour certains (en particulier la peluche symbolique du cochon rose).

Les graphismes en 2D sont jolis et colorés, beaucoup d'attention a été portée aux détails (il est possible de zoomer avec la caméra sur plusieurs plans) et l'atmosphère du jeu est très relaxante !
Cependant, j'ai trouvé que la durée du gameplay était vraiment trop courte (environ 6/7 heures), j'aurais aimé avoir plus de lieux à aménager. Ce serait par exemple agréable d'avoir non pas une seule histoire à travers tous ces lieux de déménagement, mais deux histoires supplémentaires, tout en gardant le même concept bien sûr, mais en suivant les différents déménagements et les récits personnels d'autres personnes. Pourquoi pas dans un futur jeu, qui sait ? 

J'ai également eu l'opportunité de jouer à un autre jeu sorti plus récemment qui a reproduit le même concept que "Unpacking". Il s'agit de "Camper Van : Make it Home", mais personnellement, je l'ai moins aimé.
D'une part, j'ai trouvé le gameplay plus confus, mal pensé et moins entraînant que celui-ci, et l'histoire personnelle du personnage que l'on suivait m'a moins touché, avec de nombreux éléments que je considère superflus.

C'est donc sans hésitation que je recommande ce jeu indépendant très prenant, mais à privilégier lors des promotions, car il est beaucoup trop cher à plein tarif par rapport à sa durée de jouabilité.

I played with my friends, all debating the merits of various placements as we relaxed for an afternoon. It was a lot of fun, very chill, and it was interesting seeing where we all pulled various stories elements for the items unpacked.

Unpacking feels like a very pure distillation of the idea of an "experiential" game; lots of games implement "inventory management" as a small part of a larger picture, but its rare to find a game where that is basically the sole mechanic. One example you could come up with would be Wilmot's Warehouse, but even that has a little more going on thanks to the time restrictions and upgrade system which add a little bit of mechanical depth (but it's a helpful example for our purposes here!).

This could probably be read as quite negative so far, but when utilised well, I think an absence of mechanical depth can be beneficial when something else is there to pick up the slack, and there is definitely enough going on in Unpacking to give you an engaging experience. The main goal of Unpacking's design is to give you a sincere, intimate view into the world of the games central character, who we are ostensibly playing as as we unpack boxes and arrange the contents. Her life is presented to us in a series of vignettes, wherein she has just moved into a new living space; childhood moving, university, then entering and navigating adult life, all significant bookmarks in a persons life.

Unpacking presents its story not with words, but with its environments and with our protagonists personal belongings, some of which travel with them through life, and some of which don't; be it a childhood stuffed animal that one could never see themselves parting ways with, or consumables which always end up being replenished before the next big move. Through the course of the games 5 or 6 chapters, you, the player, develop a surprisingly personal relationship to, and understanding of, our lead, and all of this is done via the simple act of (clever titledrop incoming) unpacking all of their cherished belongings.

I won't go into too much detail here, because part of the enjoyment of the experience is in uncovering and noticing these details for yourself, but I will say that Unpacking is a game with an awful lot of care invested in its crafting. I'd wager about 95% of the total of all the items you unpack in the game are totally unique, pixel-art assets (the other 5% being things like coasters), and they are complemented with a sound bank of over 14,000 files just for picking them up and putting them down on a variety of surfaces - even if a combination would make no sense for organisation, like dinnerware on a bathroom counter. You're not only free to organise the belongings however you're like, but you're encouraged to experiment, just like you might when you move into a new living space - and while progression through the story is gated by items being in the "correct" place, the game does offer accessibility options to make that process easy, or even trivial.

All in all, it's an enlightening experience and a great lesson in ludonarrative for those curious about the many, many ways in which games can be an interesting and unique story-telling medium in a way other forms of media simply can't. Highly recommend.

Original click-and-drag puzzle game uncovering stages of one person's life through the act of unpacking their possession (as you move-in to new places).

(+) Original idea
(+) Art style coherent across the whole game
(+) Levels are narratively connected and the narrative also inherently defines the level's goals (fitting all your possessions within a small space; trying to fit your things with others' who live there with you; etc.)
(+) The designers attention to describe personalities via the items they own

(-) The potential of the game is much bigger than what you'll experience
(-) A little bit too simple
(-) The space and placement restrictions feel rather frustrating than challenging
(-) The narrative is too passive, you don't affect the story/outcome whatsoever. The player could use a lot more agency as in, e.g. deciding every level between 10 things to throw away from the characters life and deciding (for the character) which new things to buy or even where to move (setting the direction of their life/the story).
(-) The gameplay focus is too binary, requiring you only to fit the things in pre-defined space. Apart from fail/success state, there's no evaluation on how you did aesthetically, how much space you saved, how much sense your layout makes (e.g. are all the gadgets accessible?)

Unpacking, ana karakterimizin çocukluğundan itibaren, hayatının farklı dönemlerinde taşındığı çeşitli evlere onun eşyalarını yerleştirdiğimiz son derece chill bir oyun. Her yeni ev, karakterimizin hayatının farklı bir dönemini temsil ediyor. Yani küçük bir kız çocuğu olarak başlayan oyun, onun mutlu bir aile kurduğu dönem ile beraber sonlanıyor. Her yeni evde, karakterimizin hayatının nasıl şekillendiğini ve çocukluğundan kalma eşyaları tekrar görmek; bu eşyaların git gide azalması bende çocukluğuma, geçmişe duyduğum özlemi ve hayatın ne kadar hızlı akıp gittiğini tekrar hatırlattı. Oynadığım her saniye içimde bir buruklukla oynadım diyebilirim. Diyalog veya sunum barındırmasa da hikayeyi oynayanın hatıraları üzerine kurmak farklı bir narrative stili olmuş. 

Kısacası Unpacking birkaç saatte biten, müzikleri tatlı, fiyatı uygun, Türkçe dil desteğine sahip hoş bir oyun. Özellikle benim gibi düzen takıntılı biriyseniz ekstra keyif alabilirsiniz.

[h1]超级放松解压的家具布置模拟器[/h1] 
《Unpacking》是一款放松向禅意益智休闲游戏。玩法十分简单，正如它的名字所示的含义一样，总结起来就是两个字：拆包。玩家所要做的事情就是拆各种各样的行李包，然后将行李包里面开出来的东西逐一摆放在房间各处。

[h1]干净了，整洁了，舒服了[/h1]
在符合正常收纳标准的情况下，因为布置的方式是自由不受限制的，玩家可以按照自己的喜好跟兴趣对行李进行摆放，所以整个游戏过程充满自定义要素，就像小时候玩扮家家酒那样，十分的有趣。除了这点外，另一个吸引人的地方那就是细节表现了。游戏内的细节十分丰富，如果玩家足够仔细的话，哪怕作者并没有直白地将故事叙述出来，玩家其实也能通过这一个个小小的细节去推测了解到出行李主人的人生故事。

[h1]满满的细节表现[/h1]
接下来简单罗列一下其中的几处细节吧。
1：从一开始各种各样的手办跟玩偶，以及卧室配色情况来看，主人公应该是一名女性（从后面出现的各种衣服跟内衣来看也能证实）。从其余物品也可以了解到她的兴趣爱好，比如喜欢看书，打游戏，喜欢听音乐，画画，喜欢踢足球（还获得了奖杯）等。
2：到了上大学后，从她在外租房跟新增的厨具来看，她应该是学会了做饭，开始了独立生活，并且紧跟时代，拥有了属于自己的第一台大头显示器电脑（好怀念啊!）。
3：到了跟别人合租的时候，因为彼此间不熟悉，处于基本的礼貌，在布置自己个人物品的时候，别人的东西基本上不能进行移动。跟后面跟男朋友同居时，男朋友的物品可以进行移动形成对比，可谓十分的真实了。
4：与男朋友分手后，为了不想起过往的伤心事，跟男友的合照是不能暴露在外面（男主的脸也被大头钉钉了起来），所以只有放在柜子里封藏才满足过关的条件（其实既然都这样了，怎么不直接扔了呢？）。
5：从最初的1997年到最后的2018年，女主使用的日常用品会随着时代的发展而更替，比如游戏机的类型， 电脑跟录音机的型号等。女主的兴趣爱好会增加，比如学会了化妆，学会了锻炼身体，养小动物等。从获得的奖项，拥有越来越多的书籍和作品，以及穿衣打扮品味上也能看出女主在变得越来越优秀跟成熟。伴随着女主珍贵物品的保留甚至也存在岁月的痕迹，比如期间小猪玩偶身上会留下缝补的记号等。
上面列举的仅仅是冰山一角，更多有意思的细节就等玩家自己去游戏内探索发现吧。

[h1]体量虽小，但趣味不低[/h1]
本作采用了关卡流程制，每个关卡对应一次新的搬家或者新的收纳。老实说，关卡数量并不是很多，如果玩家整理效率高的话，很快就能通关。但换一种心情，少一点急功近利，多一点细细品味，把它当作一款佛系游戏来看待，其实也能玩很久。因为除了过关外，游戏内还有一些有趣的要素，除了上述提到的观察细节跟自由布置外，还可以进行拍照。玩家可以对自己布置好的房间进行拍照，拍好的照片可以加上不同的滤镜，边框以及贴纸进行美化，甚至还能将自己布置房间的整个过程渲染出gif图像供欣赏。此外，游戏内还包含一些有意思的成就挑战，比如把电子产品放在危险的地方，让小木人摆出嘻哈超人姿势等。当然，最重要的是，不同年龄阶段的人去品尝这款游戏，或许都能获得不一样的滋味，感悟出不一样的道理吧。
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2649150964
[h1]总结[/h1]
清新可爱的画风，解压式的简易玩法，舒缓宁静的音乐，以及让人会心一笑的各种细节表现，总的来说这是在当今快节奏生活中不可多得的一款体量虽小巧，但上手后却意外令人着迷的“养身游戏”，感谢制作组带来的精彩小作品，同时也希望每一位玩家都能在未来的生活里收获属于自己的幸福！

A sweet little game for people who like puzzle games and/or arranging furniture. There are two points I'll say against it- There's no hint system, and it's too short. Maybe there'll be some DLC later down the track? Who knows. There's certainly some space to unpack some.

Still absolutely worth your time if you're on a first name basis with the staff at your local IKEA.

Firstly, I had hoped that this game would have been as relaxing as it looked like, and I was not disappointed. The game was very calming both in it's casual gameplay and the background music. The graphics were amazing and well done for pixel art. I am a huge fan of that art style so typically any of that kind will catch my eye, but this game offers more detailed pixel graphics. The story was subtle as it was not meant to be the forefront of the game (the unpacking and organizing was the main point). However, there is enough hints to get the gist of what had happened. I was a little bit lost in the timeline only because I ended up not paying attention to the dates as much as I should have. But, by the last stage, everything came together and made a lot more sense. So, I would say while the story is subtle and if you don't read like me, it still would be hard for someone to get lost in the story. There are some bits of the story that does make the player make inferences or fill in the gaps themselves (such as with the [spoiler]walking stick[/spoiler]). 

I didn't experience bugs/problems with the game, but I did have a small issue with the game, which was the fact that I couldn't place items where I wanted them to go and had to do more rearranging than I liked to be able to pass the stage. I didn't realize until I beat the game that there was an option to turn off the puzzle mode, which allows for more freedom in the placement of items. This is no fault of the devs, just simply me not looking at the options. It is also nice that there is an option to change the highlight color as well as the size (of what I assume is for font size). 

Overall, it was a very fun experience. Personally, I don't see any replay value for myself in this game unless more content is added. However with how relaxing the game is and the fact that you can switch out of puzzle mode, it is a game that can offer replay value for certain people. Now, the price point is a bit high for this game. Is it worth it? Yes, by all means, but if you're someone who is a bit more cautious with their spending, maybe wait for a sale. I'd still recommend it either way. It is a very nice and relaxing game for those that love casual games.

Overall, Unpacking is a cute game. The subtle storytelling is interesting, and the rooms - especially the childhood room - have a nice nostalgic feeling, but I have several gripes. First, the intended locations of the items aren't intuitive. It isn't always apparent what the items even ARE (some random box of...something?) and where they ought to go (if the towels fit in this drawer, why is that wrong?) I also didn't particularly like that the goal was literally just to get things out of the boxes and shove them into any of the allowable places regardless of convenience or aesthetic, since the end result of the room rarely actually looks nice once finished. It was also shorter than I expected, so I don't really feel that the "bang for your buck" factor is all there. Given that I finished the whole game in three hours, I really would've rather spent my money elsewhere. If you still want to try this, definitely don't purchase it at full price.

A lovely puzzle game and a masterclass in narrative without dialogue or on-screen characters. The story is told through objects and setting as you unpack and place the pieces of your life into a succession of homes. 

Every object in the game is thoughtfully designed, from sound effects and little interactive touches to subtle changes over time.  

Note that the game is short. For me, that meant three evenings' play to completion - just under five hours, with a few stickers left to go back and find.

It's cosy, romantic, clever, and casual while still feeling meaningful.

This is a really beautiful game, it really is.
It's enticing to see what a person is bringing with them each time they move, especially since this appears to be an artistic and geeky individual.  The demo amazed me; I figured we would be opening up different 'lives' and peeking into each one...but then it became clear on buying this that it's just the one life.  And while a few things do change, you are essentially unboxing the same stuffed animals, games, and clothes each time.
It's fun to see the journey, but the journey isn't that long for a $20 game.  I was hoping that each album would be another life, but once you complete the game, you can just play through again in a 'free-place' mode where you don't HAVE to put everything where the games wants you to place it.  I think it may have been more enjoyable for me if that had been a toggle-able option from the get-go, but I understand that it's a puzzle game and that the devs want you to figure things out on that first run.

I do very much recommend this to people: it's lovely, it's relaxing (for the most part), but some of the pedantic 'This must go HERE' placement restrictions on the first journey are frustrating.  I would also say this could have come at $15 and been a lot more reasonable, but I am hoping they bring in another free 'journey' or some extra content to help justify the price.  My recommendation is to wait for this to go on sale, or perhaps to see if they'll be releasing some extra content for it.

Calming, lovely art, touching story. So much information and backstory gets through without hardly any text or dialogue - a remarkable feat. I love a game where I can go at my own pace. Played this game during a time of grieving and it brought me immense comfort.

It seems that the main complaint against the game is that it's too short, considering the price. To me, it's the opposite - the game is too long. As in, it simply runs out of what keeps you engaged a little too quickly, and then it just becomes a drag. Let me elaborate.

Obviously, this is a game about unpacking the protagonist's belongings in ever changing lodgings, as she journeys through different parts of her life. So the main part that's interesting is watching her story unfold, trying to piece together the events and how she's changing over the years. This is the great part. However, the two final levels just feel like there's a whole lot of stuff to unpack in a gigantic space, while there's not so much new development. I mean, there are new things in her life; obviously I won't say what they are, but what I'm trying to say is that there's a lot of work for not much storytelling payoff.

I guess I just don't enjoy the core gameplay. "Why did you get the game?" you might ask. Well, why people play walking simulators, if all you do is walk? Because there's so much more to those games than just walking. I was hoping for a similar thing here. And indeed, the game does deliver up until a certain point; there definitely is an engaging story here, which simply slows down a little too much for my liking towards the end.

That said, when I still enjoyed the game, it was quite nice and unique. The protagonist's place in time is similar to mine, and her path in life is also not that different. Because of that, there were many nostalgic moments, many forgotten objects and places which also were part of my personal story. In a sense, it was like watching myself from a different reality, and that's a sensation not many games can evoke.

So yeah. Do you like interior design? As in, really like? Then by all means, play this. If you think this game is more than it seems to be... it sort of is, but experiencing that only makes sense if you actually enjoy the core gameplay.

On a final note... about the price. Game development is expensive. We live in a world of ever-rising housing prices, ever-stronger natural disasters and more aggressive attention economy; and the game's made in Australia, with lots of bespoke, varied pixel art, and custom music for each level. There are people who spend hundreds of (currency) on their gacha game of choice, even if those games require less effort to develop. There's a reason developers often take a "bribe" from Epic Store; because selling games simply isn't a good business model as of today. If you want this to change, bully your government into regulating this parasitic f2p nonsense; at least some of the reclaimed money would flow back into the single player market. Or perhaps it wouldn't, I'm not an economist. Hope that helps.

Unpacking is a light puzzle game themed around unpacking various items from boxes in various settings throughout some girl's life. 

To start, people often praise the light storytelling in this, but I honestly don't really see it. I understand what the game is trying to go for, and I see the little changes in items that indicate how the girl is thinking and what is currently going on in her life. However, it's simply just items and implications. I don't really find that to be an engaging way to tell a story, even if it is clever. 

Thankfully, due to the clever usage of items and clutter, we are able to understand a lot about this girl and her living situations without any text. For instance, the part where we are unpacking in a shared house with roommates resonates pretty well with me, as I'm currently in a similar situation, and finding space for items with roommates becomes tough at times. 

As for the gameplay, I think this was pretty well done for what we have to work with. The gameplay pretty much consists of taking things out of a box, finding someplace to put them, and making sure you can unpack everything in its proper places. However, there is more nuance with certain items due to being able to change their orientations or put them onto different surfaces from other items. It's a small thing, but it added greatly to the experience. 

Also, as I explained in the previous paragraph, I thought that the usage of clutter and various items helped drive certain aspects of the gameplay, such as trying to figure out what needs to go into a cupboard or what should stay on the counter. 

Sadly, the gameplay starts to become more monotonous than zen after a while, as some places make you unpack so many items to the point it feels like a chore rather than an enjoyable experience. I liked playing this game, but it just felt like things dragged on for too long due to the sheer amount of things you need to unpack. 

For the art, it is obviously an attractive aspect of this game. The high-quality pixel art really makes a lot of the items look... tasty? I don't know how to explain it, but something just looks so crisp and clean with the pixel art. It's to the point I wish I could've put food in a fridge or something to see how food would be textured. The also has a day/night cycle, so that adds even more to the overall aesthetic.

Unfortunately, even though the art is wonderful, I think the music leaves much to be desired. I honestly got a bit tired of hearing the same few tracks repeat nonstop. While the sound effects for placing items are nice, the music is just not it for me. 

Overall, I think Unpacking is a nice little game where you can just have a little fun and chill time. It isn't an amazing game as some people make it out to be, but it's still an enjoyable experience. I recommend giving this game a try if you like the vibes of it and the gameplay is something you'd enjoy. However, I don't recommend playing this game in one sitting, as I felt a bit bored after unpacking for more than an hour.

Всего предстоит обставить шесть домов (два повторяются) - от маленькой детской комнатки до здоровенного двухэтажного особняка. Каждый из них символизирует определённый этап в жизни главной героини, а по вещам можно проследить, как менялся её характер, привычки и интересы. Внешние условия тоже меняются. Например, один раз вы живёте с соседкой и её вещи передвигать не можете, приходится "встраиваться" со своим скарбом в чей-то быт. В другой раз вы въезжаете в холостяцкую берлогу своего бойфренда, где твёрдой хозяйской рукой наводите порядок.
Управление в игре элементарное. Левой кнопкой берёте вещь, правой поворачиваете, левой - ставите на положенное ей место. Иногда есть небольшой интерактив - скажем, можно включить лампу, консоль или магнитофон, собрать кубик Рубика, ткнуть в системный блок и полюбоваться на экран загрузки Windows. 
Игра очень быстро заканчивается и в этом, пожалуй, её главный недостаток. Нет, мне было интересно следить за историей героини и помогать ей обустраиваться на новом месте, но всё же за  такую цену контента маловато. Хотелось бы в конце обставить что-нибудь эпичное - кабинет президента, например, или Букингемский дворец. Надеюсь на какие-нибудь дополнения или продолжение

Unpacking è uno di quei giochi che ti conquista senza bisogno di grandi effetti speciali. Si presenta come un’esperienza cozy e rilassante, in cui l’obiettivo è semplice ma estremamente coinvolgente: spacchettare scatoloni e sistemare gli oggetti nei diversi ambienti della protagonista.

La particolarità sta nel fatto che ogni stanza e ogni oggetto raccontano, senza parole, una fase importante della vita della protagonista. Attraverso libri, vestiti, fotografie e piccoli dettagli, il giocatore ricostruisce la sua storia, seguendo il filo delle tappe più significative.

L’ambientazione è tenera e curata in ogni minimo particolare: la grafica 3D, colorata e stilizzata, trasmette calore e intimità, trasformando ogni livello in una piccola finestra sulla quotidianità. Non c’è fretta né competizione: il ritmo lento e meditativo permette di rilassarsi e allo stesso tempo riflettere sul significato che gli oggetti assumono nelle nostre vite.

------
Unpacking is one of those games that wins you over without the need for flashy effects. It presents itself as a cozy and relaxing experience, where the goal is simple yet deeply engaging: unpack boxes and place the items in the protagonist’s different living spaces.

What makes it special is that every room and every object silently tells a part of the protagonist’s life story. Through books, clothes, photographs, and small details, the player gradually pieces together her journey, following the milestones that shaped her life.

The atmosphere is tender and carefully crafted: the colorful, stylized 3D graphics convey warmth and intimacy, turning each level into a small window into everyday life. There’s no rush, no competition—just a slow, meditative pace that allows you to relax while reflecting on the meaning that objects carry in our lives.

Unpacking is a cozy and relaxing puzzle game focusing on the unpacking of boxes and decorating of spaces as you watch a woman’s life unfold.

The game is divided into multiple chapters, the first one being the year 1997. You start out by helping a young girl decorate her very first own room, and from then on, you follow along her life as she moves out and moves places. You get to watch her story through little details while unpacking and organizing her new living spaces — details such as which items she keeps, which ones disappear throughout the years, and even which ones reappear later on.


While the possibilities when decorating are technically limited, they tend to feel endless at times, leaving space for a lot of creative freedom. I only ever had issues placing an item once, but was able to solve it quickly enough.

The pixel art is lovely to look at and feels less straining on the eyes than other games with similar graphics.


Unfortunately, the game is too pricey for its length. The full game, including obtaining all achievements, takes about three hours maximum. Therefore I would only recommend getting it on sale.

I would’ve wished for either multiple storylines or more chapters — even an ‘unlimited mode’ would’ve satisfied me more than enough.

Another issue is that the decorated rooms will unfortunately end up looking cluttered at times, which was something that annoyed me just a little, as there’s no option to make everything look tidy sometimes.


The game overall tends to be a relaxing experience and is definitely worth to try out, although said experience is unfortunately over too quickly.

Grafika jest prześliczna, poziomy progresywnie stają się większe i bardziej rozbudowane idealnie komplementując dorastanie głównej bohaterki zarówno jak naszych umiejętności do rozkładania rzeczy. Ukryte osiągnięcia sprawiają, że aż chce się w tą grę zagrać ponownie (co ja sama zrobiłam wielokrotnie), a muzyka jest tak pasująca, że ani razu nie miałam ochoty włączyć własnej playlisty w tle.

Odkrywamy historie dzięki małym szczegółom i przedmiotom które układamy, co jest idealnym rozwiązaniem które pozwala gameplayowi być głównym aspektem, jednocześnie nie pozostawiając gracza z pytaniem "czyje rzeczy ja w ogóle rozkładam?", równocześnie zostawiając wystarczająco przestrzeni na własną interpretacje bardziej szczegółowych aspektów.

Podsumowując, gra jest spokojna, estetyczna, miła dla oka i ucha. Osobiście uważam, że posiada replayability value, chociaż raczej po jakimś czasie, gdy się zapomni gdzie co się ułożyło poprzednio.

"Unpacking" is a deeply personal and heartfelt game that speaks to the essence of who we are through the act of unpacking. It invites players to reflect on their own experiences and memories as they meticulously arrange items in various rooms. The game beautifully captures the emotions and nostalgia associated with moving and settling into a new space. Each object tells a story, from cherished mementos to everyday items, evoking a sense of warmth and familiarity. The attention to detail in the game is astonishing, with every item carefully crafted and meticulously placed. Through its minimalist gameplay and stunning pixel art, "Unpacking" creates an intimate connection with the player, eliciting both joy and melancholy. It reminds us of the significance of the spaces we inhabit and the power of objects to evoke emotions and memories.

A very charming, lovely game. You learn a lot about someone just by unpacking the stuff they own. A nice feature the game contains is the ability to watch a playback of your work once it's complete! Love all the sound effects that come with moving and placing items you get to hear. It's a giant puzzle that you get to really feel for and learn to love as you progress further into Unpacking. While the price of the game seems a little absurd with how many hours of game play you get (5 hr for full completion), it is worth it for the love the creator obviously put in making the story and game mechanics. While there isn't a lot of replay value, there is some if you just want to continue organizing to your hearts content. I recommend this game to people who wanna stick around for a slice of life story and for some fun, relaxing puzzle solving.

Super calming , relaxing game.
But, I haven't seen anyone talk about the "character" you play through.
The best part for me was kind of inferring about her life. You start with her childhood bedroom, and then you move to what looks like a dorm room, and then into a house that already has men's stuff established. Next you're back at her parents house, and you can assume it didn't work out, and then you're out on your own again in a shabbier looking place, etc. As you move through the levels, you even get new stuff to put in a place you've already been, and we get to see her personality and hobbies flesh out without ever interacting with a single character. Like, oh, now she's into gardening? She upgraded her make-up to a more professional set? Her work uniform changed, did she get a new job?
It's a super cute, and I love that you get to imagine an invisible character's personal life (even if it is through putting up her tampons)

Edit: Just finished the game, I was so naive, lol. Good game, takes about 5 hours to complete.

Das Game macht unglaublich viel Spass - ist ein absoluter Entspannungshelfer und man kann richtig schön runter fahren. Zumindest für 2,5 Stunden - danach war das Spiel durch und man denkt sich, wofür man eben noch Geld ausgegeben hat. Unpacking macht so vieles richtig, mit einem tollen Setting und auch einer wirklich guten Umsetzung. Was bei Die Sims noch zu Oberflächlich ist, wird bei Unpacking dafür um so detailverliebter. Wirklich jedes Messer oder jedes Buch will einzeln in die Regale oder Möbel geräumt werden. Dabei ist der Phantasie fast keine grenzen gesetzt. Nur manchmal meckert das Spiel wenn falsche Objekte in falschen Räumen platziert sind. Ansonsten hat man zu 95 % die freie Gestaltungsmöglichkeit.
Leider tröstet das aber nicht über die extrem kurze Spielzeit hinaus - nach knapp 2,5 Stunden ist man durch ohne das man sich hetzen muss. Denn das Spielprinzip ist so einfach gehalten dass es einem ohne Probleme von der Hand geht.
Leider gibt es aktuell keinen Mod Support oder neue Levels, es gibt auch keinen Sandbox Mode oder dergleichen - nach 8 Level ists dann schon wieder vorbei.
Ich habe für das Spiel im Sale 15.- Euro bezahlt, kann aber nur empfehlen zu warten bis es nochmal weniger kostet. Für den mauen Inhalt gebe ich dem Spiel einen roten Daumen - obwohl es wirklich super gemacht ist. Aber Preis/Leistung passt hier definitiv nicht.

7/10 Unpacking is a simple and heart wrenchingly relatable puzzle type game where you must unpack a person's belongings into their room as they go through new stages of life. Beautiful, simple, and very cute.

My takeaway: Unpacking was a game I just had to have. It combines beautiful storytelling with gameplay that will itch your brain in all the right ways. It’s challenging and will pull on your heart strings. I think anyone who has left home can relate in some way to the main character and the story they tell solely on her belongings and environment is very impressive. 

The art is stunning and the game goes off without a hitch. Very good at explaining things to you without making you feel like a child with relaxing music to go along with it. Despite all these praises the price is hefty for a game that took me a little under three hours to fully complete, achievements and all. Normally a good rule of thumb is to expect an hour's worth of content for every dollar spent but despite being short, with 7 levels, it’s exceptional at what it does right.

[u]Pros[/u]
[list]
   [*] Beautiful storytelling told in a very unique way.
   [*] The art is perfect for this type of game and gives off a great atmosphere!
   [*] The soundtrack is so good!
   [*] Achievements.
   [*] Trading cards.
   [*] No rush gameplay that allows you to take your time and think.
   [*] Leaves you wanting more.
[/list]

[u]Cons[/u]
[list]
   [*] Extremely short with no plans to lengthen. 
[/list]

[h1]a cute game about the things that fill up our homes and our hearts :)[/h1]

everything the player character owns tells pieces of a story, and every move into a new place is the beginning of a new chapter that slowly paints a portrait of the person they grow into. 

this game is very easy to just jump in and complete quickly if that's how you'd like to play it, but it's also relaxing to dive into what each item means to the person who owns it and place everything with purpose and care. there's even an option to remove the (already very open ended!) puzzle feature and just place things wherever you'd like, but I would recommend not doing so as it is really the only "challenge" that the game has and since things are still never fully [i]locked[/i] to one spot, it's just more of a guideline system.

I thoroughly enjoyed the music in each move, and the sound design that went into this game was so obviously a labor of love that shows in the incredible detail given to the individual sounds of the items you place. every sound is so accurate that any fidelity lost in the translation of the game's pixel design was made up for by the fact that you could hear exactly what you were picking up and what it was sitting on.

in summary, my only complaint isn't even a complaint at all, I just wish there were more levels to unpack because I enjoyed every moment of playing this game and I fully recommend picking it up if you like calm, 'play at your own pace' type games that let you fill in the blanks of the story through personal discovery.

Une expérience originale et émouvante. 
Unpacking est un petit jeu de déménagement au pitch en apparence très simple mais qui renferme une grande profondeur. On y explore la vie d'une jeune femme, de son enfance à l'âge adulte, à travers ses divers déménagements. On l'accompagne tout au long des étapes marquantes de sa vie, tout en découvrant au fur et à mesure qui elle est, ce qu'elle aime et où elle va. 
Le [i]gameplay[/i] est simple mais très bien exécuté. Les possibilités de rangement sont nombreuses et je ne suis jamais tombée sur une incohérence au cours de toutes mes heures de jeu. La musique et le [i]sound design[/i] sont excellents. Le [i]pixel art[/i] est beau. Tout dans ce jeu m'a ravi. La narration se fait par l'environnement et l'on découvre toujours un peu plus de la vie de l'héroïne au fil des [i]unpackings[/i]. 
C'est un jeu fabuleux (et je pèse mes mots) que je ne peux que recommander !

I wanted this game as soon as I saw it teased somewhere online. Aside from the fact that the game feeds into our deep-seeded need to organize things, unpacking provides a deep look at what the objects we continually surround ourselves with tell our story. Life is merely a collection of memories and accumulated "stuff". Seeing the story of the protagonist unfold as the years went by not only impressed me in how so much could be told without so much as seeing a single human-being for the runtime of the game, but also made me reflect on my own life and the things that I hold on to. Time and time again I find that the games that make the largest impact on me are those that are small, indie-developed titles that are not afraid to make a statement within unconventional game design. Unpacking stands a testament to what can be done with video games as an art form. I look forward to what Witchbeam produces next!

Witch Beam pulled off some magic in this game.

Its simple, relaxing, has a touching story that doesn't need cutscenes or really any writing to come across. It hits that lovely small-game sweet spot of long enough to get its goals done - short enough to not wear out its welcome. While some folks complain that its too short for the price - you're paying for polish in this game.

If you're looking for something to kill 20 hours, this isn't the game for you. But if you're looking for a relaxing experience that makes you think and appreciate the art of game design - don't pass this one up.

To the creators - Keep making things. I don't want Unpacking 2, but I want to see how your studio builds and grows. I look forward to your next game, and hope it shines as bright as this one.

Before I get into the details, I want to mention about the price. I personally think the game is overpriced for this kind of game mechanism (a bit pixelated, lacking of variety of items, short gameplay). I think the only reason that this game cost high is because they’re selling ‘the idea’. This kind of zen puzzle game is something that would interest anyone who would want to find peace, calm and relaxing game and I’m the one who enjoy this kind of game. 

[h1]THE GAMEPLAY[/h1]

Never felt so stressed out playing a game that was meant to be relaxing. Maybe it's just not for me, but despite the offers of accessibility options, I really couldn't play the game how I wanted or expected.
You can either choose to place things wherever you want or (the recommended option) have it be a puzzle to solve, where objects must go in a specific place. I wanted it to be a puzzle, so I went for that, but the experience was bad and couldn't be changed through accessibility options.
Problem 1: The flashing outline around objects hurt my eyes. It may not be rapid flashing but I do have issues with flashing lights and had to take constant breaks. This outline only appears if you unpack every box so I started leaving one box closed so I wouldn't have to deal with it. However that lead to another issue.
Problem 2: The flashing room UI. Basically, if you have a room in the house that has an unopened box, your HUD will start flashing. There was no way I could see in the options that I could turn it off, and it distracted me from unpacking. It's strange to put what is essentially a big flashing timer on a game that a) has no timer and b) is supposed to be relaxing. I really wanted to turn that off.

This is minor but also the music was not great. I don't usually ever have an issue with music in games, I'm easy to please. But it got to the point where I had to just put my own music on and mute the game music because of how repetitive it got. Maybe that's just me, I'm sure the OST is on YT so it's easy to check if it's up your alley.

I left the game on for a while at one point when I had to get up and let my eyes rest so my play time is a little off, its probably closer to 4-5 hours.
Also I love the pixel art but some objects are very hard to tell what they are and I couldn't for the life of me tell where they were supposed to go. It came down to me randomly placing the object everywhere until it eventually let me.
Like the last level had this tube of what looked like cream/moisturiser. I tried it in the bathroom: nope. In the OTHER bathroom? Nope. Eventually I found a place for it (in one of the bedrooms for some reason) and just left it there so I could move on with my life even if it looked bad.

Tldr: My advice for how best to play this game would be to choose placing objects wherever you want, and with the music turned off and having your own soundtrack on. It's clear this game has love put into it so I'm not bashing it, I'm just reviewing it like this in case there's others who have issues with the flashing lights like I do, because that might be a deal breaker.

Unpacking is one of those games that feels like a warm hug without saying a single word. On the surface, you’re just opening boxes and placing objects in a home. But as you go through each stage — childhood bedrooms, student dorms, shared apartments, independent living — you start piecing together someone’s entire life through the little things they own. It’s quiet, simple, and incredibly emotional.

Gameplay
The mechanics couldn’t be more straightforward: you unpack boxes and figure out where everything should go. Each level represents a different stage of life, and by putting items in their right (or sometimes not-so-right) places, you slowly build a story. No timers, no competition, just the gentle puzzle of arranging a life. It’s peaceful, almost meditative, but also surprisingly deep.

Look and sound
The pixel art is soft and cozy, but the real magic is in the sound design. Every single object has its own unique sound effect when you pick it up or put it down — cups clink differently from plates, clothes fold softly, keyboards clatter just right. These tiny details make the whole experience tactile and personal. It’s like you can feel the objects through the audio.

Storytelling and themes
There’s no dialogue, barely any text. The story is told entirely through objects: a poster taped to the wall, a beloved plush toy, medicine bottles, photo frames. The game is all about identity, growth, heartbreak, joy — how our belongings carry who we are. Some moments hit hard, others feel comforting, but all of them are quietly powerful.

Accessibility and flow
It’s short — just a few hours — but that’s part of its charm. It’s replayable if you want to rearrange things or just revisit certain life stages. And it’s very accessible: simple controls, relaxed pacing, almost no language barriers. It really feels designed for anyone to step in and feel something.

Final thoughts
Unpacking is tender, melancholic, and strangely healing. It turns a mundane chore into art, and it leaves you reflecting on your own life, your own rooms, your own boxes. It’s not flashy, it’s not dramatic, but it’s one of those experiences that stay with you. Honestly, it’s comfort in pixels — the kind of game you’ll want to revisit when you just need a little bit of warmth.

The game’s gorgeous aesthetics and gentle gameplay create a serene atmosphere, making each level feel like a cozy, intimate journey. As you unpack items and arrange them in different settings, subtle, emotional moments emerge, telling a heartfelt story without a single line of dialogue.

It's easy to become attached to the main character's life, making the experience both nostalgic and unexpectedly moving. My only wish is that it lasted longer, as I found myself wanting to stay in this world a little while more.

"Unpacking" has beautiful and engaging environmental storytelling, with details such as [spoiler] the number of chick statuettes and the country souvenirs multiplying over the years to indicate the main character's interests as well as to signify the passage of time. It was also a very smart move to show the dysfunction of the main character's relationship with the boyfriend by making the only available space for her diploma, a symbol of her achievements and hard work, at the very bottom of the closet. [/spoiler] However, I felt that the game was too short for me to fully enjoy the environmental storytelling. I was able to finish the game in one sitting, with plenty of time just to see if there were any alternative item placements. I did not feel like I had enough time to get the know the main character, their career, [spoiler] their relationship with their girlfriend (other than that it presumably is good, as they end up having a baby) [/spoiler]; I did not feel like I had time to truly care for this character's story. 

Moreover, the game has a charming pixel art style that nice to look at, but this art style also makes objects hard to recognize. Some objects took a solid minute of me staring to understand what it is, and some I put randomly on surfaces until they stopped registering as "misplaced". This frustration really takes away (in my opinion) from the relaxing atmosphere the game is trying to foster with the art style and soundtrack (which are very enjoyable!).

In the end, this game feels more like a demo to me than a full game. Taking "environmental storytelling" to the extreme by telling the story of the main character through the objects they own and how they place them is genius. But it lacks in execution with the shortness of the whole experience. Once you start really getting invested in this person's story, it's already over, and that's a real shame.

Do I regret the time I spent on this game? Absolutely not. But would I recommend buying it, especially at the price point I bought the game? Unfortunately, no, not really. I would say go for it if it is on sale or if the mechanic of organizing rooms interests you, but aside from those, I wouldn't recommend it.

爆炸级的音效设计！当女主开始与其他人合租时间，由于并不存在亲密关系，因此只能触碰和摆放自己的物品。和男友同居开始所有物品都可以交互，但非常有趣的是和第一位男友同居时男生的物品拜访的很有侵略性——是男主自己的住所，女主是外来的客人的感觉。很多洗漱用品、内衣空间都被占据，我这种不能接受内裤和袜子放一起的强迫症于是开始整理两人的东西，难免感受到作者想传递的“繁杂家务”和“疏离亲密”——两个人同居了，但生活并没有彼此融入。当女主后来和另一位女生居住时，二人的共同爱好开始彼此交集，共用的手写板、一起买的很多游戏、两个人都喜欢的家居装饰等等。

第二点是，所有的可点击物品都有自己的独特音效，最让我震撼的是女孩小时候用的卫生棉条和长大了用的不是同一个品牌，一个是棉花包裹的packing，后来升级成了圆柱塑料壳，而这两种卫生棉在点击放置时候的声音好像是有微小差别的（也有可能是另一种药品，像素太小看不清。。但即使维生素药丸和膏药贴也是能细致地听出差别的，太赞了）。不掩饰的女性&喜欢女性的视角，虽然也感受到了一些对男性的厌恶，不知作者是刻意为之制造冲突还是用了真实的记忆。难免揣测是后者;   ; ，希望她好好的。

总之用时3.4h打了非全成就通关，应该会回去打全成就，安静地听（看）完了片尾曲，感觉这种细腻的作者一定会把自己童年最喜欢的人放到鸣谢，果然看到了作者祖母的名字hhh  ''We unpack our life, I smile to myself''


此时此刻难免回忆起一些命题贴：你能接受对方和别人同居过很久吗？大家似乎更多地关心性、精神和肉体，彼此纠缠的非物质层面，但我更害怕的是没有跟对方走下去，分开之后带来的日常侵蚀感。

unpacking将这种感觉发挥到了极致，一个非常注重家居细节的人，女主人的锅、冰箱贴、围裙、最喜欢的几本书和小猪娃娃是她从始至终带在身边的物品，同居男友不在乎她，因此没有对她的任何爱好/兴趣/成就进行过处理——这里我倾向于作者保留了一种理想化的脱离假设，只要男友把自己的奖杯和勋章丢到床下，那么这段感情就是纯粹的冷漠与失败；正是因为她无法假设相爱过的同居情侣将怎样分开，女主和最终在一起的女友共同创造了非常非常多温馨的家庭环境。包括女主的冰箱贴爱好，而对方也接纳并融合了，买了很多可以跟女主的冰箱贴联系起来的字母和小动物。

这和记忆不一样，当一件物品因为爱出现在你的生活里朝夕相伴，那么这就意味着你完全地将自己没有防备的家园领土拱手相让，并天真地祈望二人永远不会分开。希望世人都能得到如此美妙梦想。

Okay so, first and foremost, this game is *adorable*.  You play the part of an invisible female character as she unpacks after moving and sets up her space(s) in a number of different new living quarters.  The graphics are crisp and clean, the music is relaxing, the sound effects are on point, and, if you are into space management and orderly games, you'll probably find this game cathartic and oddly satisfying, for the most part.  Some of the achievements are hilarious ([spoiler] try putting your flattening iron in the sink or bathtub![/spoiler]) and, although there are no instructions or dialogue, there's still a clear story to be followed that will trigger your feels; also, watching your character's belongings evolve and change as they grow up and their priorities shift is more fun than you would think.

I have a few mild grievances, but, personally, none of them would really have impacted my decision to purchase the game.  There are conditions for clearing each stage that are not always easy to figure out how to satisfy.  (As an example, in the first stage, [spoiler]your character will not be happy unless her diary is 'hidden' in a drawer or cabinet[/spoiler].)  There are more complicated examples of this later, and some of them are not intuitive at all and took me some time to puzzle out.  

With that aside, I could also make an argument that the game doesn't feel entirely done (or, at a minimum, that it has more potential that wasn't used) because there are a lot of things you *can't* do that I feel would enhance its enjoyment.  I would have been much happier if I was able to move furniture or discard/store items, for example.  ([spoiler]What if I don't like visual clutter and don't want 17 fridge magnets?[/spoiler])  A casual mode that isn't storyline-based would also be a fun addition if they continued to do more work on it, but it seems like it's a completed project that won't get anymore content.

Anyway, overall, it's a fun and satisfying game, and I don't regret my purchase.  Some people have taken fault with the cost for what it is (I'm on the last stage in less than 4 hours of playtime), and although this doesn't personally bother me - I'm happy to support a small studio of developers - I would probably wait for a sale to purchase this if I could go back in time.

Unpacking is a relaxing puzzle game where you unpack boxes throughout different stages of your life. The mode of storytelling is unique and engaging, while remaining truthful and relatable. The story is told through objects, sound, and surroundings- we never see the character we play as, nor do we see anyone else in their life, for that matter. What we do see are the impacts of time, surroundings, and people as we evolve. In this way, Unpacking is one of the most human games I have played. Additionally, there is more than one way to play: if you prefer placing each item where it belongs with the game's limitations, the puzzle aspect comes into play a bit more strongly. If you prefer to place each item wherever you want without the game's limitations, then just make that adjustment in the settings. As of now, I have completed the game twice, earned every achievement, and am halfway through a third run- and my honest opinion is that it's incredibly apparent that a great deal of thought and care was put into this game; from visual design to storytelling, to sound design, to level design. I would recommend Unpacking to anyone. 

Some people who have reviewed this game have expressed that the elements of gender and sexuality portrayed in Unpacking lacked relatability to them. To this, I would say that the point of the game is to find a place for your belongings and experience the familiarity of establishing and re-establishing yourself throughout different stages of life, and the player doesn't need the gender or sexuality of the character to reflect their own in order for the point of the game to hit home. That said, I wouldn't judge someone who feels that this aspect makes it difficult for them to enjoy Unpacking- my only hope is that reading those reviews wouldn't necessarily deter anyone else from taking a chance on this game.

It's a fine concept but for the price tag the game does not have even close to as much content as I would want. I want more characters with different possessions, and more levels for the one character we do have. This is a jaded thumbs up.  The game is unique and interesting to play.  However, there is no help or instructions and the game is not intuitive. On the first few levels, you unpack boxes in each room and all the things in the boxes belong in that room, so it's just a matter of finding a spot for all the objects - easy enough at first.  As you progress, you unpack one room and put items away, then move to another  room, and you'll discover objects which clearly belong in different rooms (you have to start memorizing what sort of objects go where). As things go along, you find that some objects, even in the room where they belong, must be in a particular place (and for no apparent reason).  At this point It gets more irritating than fun.  And then, it's over!  This big build up, and for what?  The story line was somewhat interesting, if you're interested in that sort of thing, but in this kind of game, it didn't add anything - it was as if the developers were trying to make a statement [from 40 years ago]:  Girl grows up, Girl has dreams, Girl falls in love, Girl gets heart broken, Girl get hurt/has medical problems, Girl accomplishes different dream, Girl finds true love with another Girl and true happiness.  (Frankly, I find it passe.)  The game is short, no matter how much you fumble around with the goods and the boxes, (finished first time in 2.6 hours then went for 6 missing achievements) and as for the secret achievements - well, I got most of them by accident, then pretty much guessed the rest by trial and error, again, there is no help with how to interact with objects. I don't think the game is worth the full price being asked.  I purchased on sale, so my tears aren't too bitter.

  I wanted this game to be relaxing and stress relieving, but it actually turned out to be the opposite in certain places. The goal of the game is extremely simple; you unpack boxes and place the items around a room. In some levels there are more than one room, with items that fit that room (example, a kitchen and some of the items you pull out of the boxes being pots, kitchen utensils, etc). What I didn't like is there are certain items that have specific locations they need to be placed, but the game doesn't actually tell you where they want those items, so you have to go room to room moving the item around and hoping that you find the right place. Another thing that I didn't like is that I like clean and clutter-free spaces, but there is one specific level where the house you're moving into is extremely cluttered, so trying to unpack the huge volume of boxes the game gives you is just stressful because there isn't any room to put stuff. You can't move items that are already placed in the level- you can only move items that you're unpacking from the boxes (this prevented me from organizing the room and freeing up space to unpack).

Overall it's a well designed game, but the strictness of the placement of some items and the cluttered areas you're unpacking into made me return the game. I would still recommend it to most people though, as I think my situation is a pretty unique one.

Unpacking is exactly what you expect, no clickbait, no anything, you just unpack stuff outta boxes as you move into a new home, and you have to do it right. So no, you don't put a ruler under your pillow to measure your ♥♥♥♥ size every morning, no, you don't store a toaster in your bathtub. 

Everything has a place.

The game lets you live through a story, while not telling you much about it. The one sentence after you beat a level & all the photos and boxes tell you the story. That's quite cute, you don't have to care for the story, it is just a nice detail.

When it comes to the graphics, the graphics are pixelated, which is one of the reasons that make the game unique. It has such a charming, vibrant art style, but occasionally you can't decipher what you're holding, so you just put it on random shelves until the game tells you the job is done. At least the game tells you what's wrong, but there are definitely moments in the game in which you just keep doing trial & error.

Many times you also find a reference or two, especially consoles and handhelds are prevalent easter eggs. If you know, you know, and that is the rule the game goes by.

The levels are mostly fun, while I had problems with one or two, they were immediately fixed by some that are just a bit different and mix up the formula. I gotta say, the game ended at the right moment, no wishing for more, no chores, exactly when I thought I've seen enough, the game ended.

Unpacking is one of those unique indie games that you wouldn't see by any big publisher. Sometimes things as little as unpacking boxes turn the switch and make it fun, cozy, but most importantly oddly entertaining.

3/10, I did not like this game at all and couldn't bring myself to finish it for multiple reasons.

I walked in thinking that it would be a calming organization sim in which you would be able to choose where you want to put things. Instead, it acts like a puzzle game, in which you are given a ton of items and very limited space to put them, a trait only exacerbated by the fact that there are perfectly reasonable places for items that are just completely invalid for some reason.

I know that there is an option to enable "put things wherever," but for some reason it's under accessibility, which seems like a not-so-subtle nudge by the devs to make you feel incompetent for not following their rules. The original, unaltered version of the game feels less like a game of choice and aesthetic freedom and more like a "guess where the game wants you to put this doll" simulator.

I also feel like the choice to make the items sort of "reveal" the personality of the character that, I guess, you are playing as(?), was a somewhat bad decision. Part of the draw of the concept of a game built around organization is that in organization you can express yourself, a bit like art. In forcing the items to be very specific to the character you are organizing for it takes away some of the creative potential of the game in my opinion.

Overall a good premise with subpar execution and a lot of iffy design choices. I wouldn't buy unless you like somewhat unintuitive puzzles and would relate a lot to the character you are organizing for.
