[b]Un juego con encanto y personalidad[/b]

[i]Unpacking[/i] es un juego con un notable encanto y personalidad, acompañado de unos bonitos [b]gráficos[/b] en 2D que capturan la atención de inmediato. La [b]mecánica[/b] central, que consiste en organizar y colocar objetos en diferentes espacios, está bien implementada y resulta muy satisfactoria. La variedad de objetos a colocar y los diferentes lugares donde hacerlo mantienen el juego interesante y permiten una experiencia entretenida mientras avanzamos.

Los [b]escenarios[/b] interactivos, como la capacidad de abrir puertas y cajones, contribuyen al dinamismo del juego y refuerzan la sensación de inmersión en el entorno. Sin embargo, aunque la vista isométrica cumple con su función, a veces eché de menos un enfoque en 3D. En ciertas ocasiones, hubiera preferido poder girar ligeramente la [b]cámara[/b], lo que habría facilitado la visualización de espacios más cerrados, como armarios o estanterías.

El [b]fondo[/b] del escenario, es decir, lo que no es parte de la escena interactuable, se queda corto y resulta un tanto aburrido. Una mayor creatividad en esta área habría mejorado la experiencia visual general.

Por otro lado, los [b]efectos de sonido[/b] son excepcionales. Aunque los gráficos son sencillos, el sonido aporta un contraste muy agradable y realista, además de servir como pista cuando no queda claro dónde colocar algún objeto. Este toque sonoro eleva la atmósfera del juego de manera significativa.

Los [b]logros[/b], representados en forma de “stickers”, son una adición creativa y bien integrada dentro del juego. Me gusta especialmente que los logros no se sientan ajenos al desarrollo del juego, sino que se incorporen de manera fluida y divertida.

Unpacking es un juego entretenido, ideal para pasar el rato y disfrutar de la historia que se va desarrollando mientras descubrimos el progreso de nuestro personaje. Sin embargo, el [b]final[/b] me dejó con una sensación de [b]abrupto[/b] cierre. Quizás habría sido interesante un nivel pequeño adicional que diera un cierre más apropiado a la evolución del relato.

Aunque se promociona como un juego libre, sin presiones ni tiempos, cabe señalar que algunos objetos tienen un lugar limitado donde deben ir para ser considerados "correctos" y avanzar al siguiente nivel. Esto puede restar un poco de [b]libertad[/b] a la experiencia, aunque no interfiere demasiado en la jugabilidad.

[b]En resumen[/b], [i]Unpacking[/i] es una propuesta refrescante y agradable, con mecánicas simples pero efectivas, y un toque creativo que lo hace único. Aunque algunas áreas podrían haberse mejorado, sigue siendo una opción muy recomendable para quienes buscan una experiencia tranquila y satisfactoria.

Unpacking é um daqueles jogos que parecem simples demais no começo, mas que acabam surpreendendo. A ideia é basicamente tirar objetos das caixas e organizar cada cômodo, mas o jogo consegue transformar isso em uma experiência muito gostosa e relaxante.

O mais legal é que, enquanto organizamos as coisas, também acompanhamos diferentes momentos da vida da protagonista. Sem precisar de grandes diálogos ou cenas, os próprios objetos vão contando a história.

A pixel art é simples, mas muito bonita, e os pequenos detalhes dos ambientes deixam tudo ainda mais interessante. Também é muito satisfatório ver cada cômodo ficando organizado depois de terminar uma fase.

É um jogo curto e não tem grandes desafios, então talvez não agrade quem procura muita ação. Mas, para quem gosta de experiências tranquilas e de jogos que contam histórias de uma maneira diferente, Unpacking vale muito a pena.

Nota: 8,5/10.

Плюсы:
- милое пиксельное визуальное оформление
- релакс-геймплей
- хорошая фоновая музыка
- есть мини "пасхалки", за поиски которых даются достижения

Минусы: 
- коротенькая (максимум можно растянуть прохождение на 5 часов, и то — если вы очень неторопливо занимаетесь обставлением комнат и разглядыванием вещей)
- для предметов есть заранее продуманное место разработчиками, т.е. туалетную бумагу не удастся спрятать под подушку. На самом деле, я этот минус увидела у кого-то в обзоре, но лично я не считаю это большим недостатком, так как мы в первую очередь пытаемся навести порядок, и было бы странно, если бы игра давала возможность рандомно раскидывать предметы, тогда геймплей сократился бы минимум вдвое-трое. Но вдруг для кого-то это важно, поэтому пусть будет.
- я пару раз за игру встречала вещи, предназначение которых мне было непонятно, а вследствие возникал небольшой тупняк с тем, чтобы найти им правильное место. Возможно это был чисто мой прикол и критичным я это тоже не назову. 

Вывод: если хотите устроить себе cozy relax вечерок, советую к приобретению, особенно во время скидок!

„Unpacking“ ist der Beweis, dass man keine Explosionen, Kämpfe oder Dialoge braucht, um eine tiefgehende Geschichte zu erzählen. Das Spiel wirkt auf den ersten Blick simpel – man packt Umzugskartons aus und räumt Dinge in eine neue Wohnung ein. Doch in dieser Schlichtheit entfaltet sich eine unerwartet emotionale, intime und wunderschön erzählte Geschichte.

Ohne ein einziges gesprochenes Wort oder Text erzählt Unpacking das Leben einer Person über verschiedene Lebensabschnitte hinweg – vom Kinderzimmer über die erste Studentenwohnung bis hin zum eigenen Zuhause. Jeder Gegenstand, den man aus den Kisten holt, erzählt ein Stück Biografie: Erinnerungen, Erfolge, Rückschläge, Beziehungen, Neubeginne.
So wird das Aufräumen zu einem Puzzle der Persönlichkeit – meditativ, beruhigend und zugleich erstaunlich tief.

Der Pixel-Art-Stil ist liebevoll bis ins Detail gestaltet, die Soundkulisse ist sanft und realistisch – vom Rascheln des Packpapiers bis zum Klick der Schublade. Dieses Spiel schafft es, dass man beim Platzieren einer Zahnbürste oder eines Fotos plötzlich innehalten und lächeln (oder seufzen) muss.

Fazit:
Unpacking ist eine stille Meisterleistung, die zeigt, dass große Emotionen auch in den kleinsten Dingen liegen können. Es ist gleichzeitig entspannend, nachdenklich und zutiefst menschlich – ein Spiel, das nicht laut sein muss, um Eindruck zu hinterlassen.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5)

On parle ici, d’un petit jeu détente qui peut vite amener à l'addiction ! 

Vous rêvez que tout soit bien rangé à sa place lors d'un aménagement ? Votre âme maniaque et votre quête de perfection est sans limite ? Ce jeu est fait pour vous !

Le but est de sortir du carton les affaires et de les ranger, sans limite de temps et sans score ! Il faut tout simplement ranger les affaires correctement et que cela soit en adéquation avec votre gout ! Laissez vous porter par les différentes missions qui semblent raconter l’histoire d’une jeune demoiselle.

C'est à vous d'imaginer sa vie et son histoire mais il y aura des indices tout au long du jeu qui vous permettrons d'en savoir plus sur sa vie et ses événements de vie !

Au total vous aurez 8 déménagements à faire, plus quelques petits défis à réaliser si vous êtes assez curieux.

Ce jeu conviendra parfaitement aux personnes recherchant un petit jeu de détente, ou simplement pour des enfants par exemple.

(N.B. while Steam might say I played for 4h at the time of writing, I did watch someone else play through most of the game on stream prior to playing it myself, so that play time is likely on the shorter side. I'd recommend taking your time, as the charm of this game is in the details.)

This is one of those games which I would have loved if not for one very specific flaw. In this case, it's that each level ends with having to move any item which is in a spot that it shouldn't be. On its own this wouldn't be too bad, but the problem is that it doesn't really explain itself beyond outlining items that aren't in an acceptable spot, which means that it's a read-the-devs'-minds puzzle, which is one of the worst failures of game design. And to make it even worse, the fact that that's the last part of each move before it's properly "complete" means that for me it sours the whole experience of the gameplay leading up to it in a way that bad gameplay interludes usually don't for me.
And it's a real shame that that's the case, because aside from that it's an absolutely incredible game, with an interesting premise that's very well-executed. The gameplay consists of dragging and dropping items from moving boxes as the player character unpacks after each time they move to a new living space, without ever seeing what you actually look like or directly learning details of who you are. The combination of the quite mundane activity defining gameplay and the way that information is only presented about the character you are notionally playing as gives a quite poignant combination of mystery and intimate emotional connection, and if you take it at all seriously the act of unpacking demands just enough thought to keep you engaged without being frustrating or distracting you from the storytelling. I was genuinely invested in the protagonist's story and wanting to see how it develops, but the cleanup at the end of each level is just so frustrating that it ruined the game for me despite that appeal.

Unpacking ticks a lot of boxes: 
- It's a relaxing, cosy game that's very replayable;
- While it's not stressful, there is still an element of challenge (item placement is restricted i.e. leaving things on the floor, but this can be switched off so you have complete freedom); and
- The visuals and sound design add to it's beauty and the 'story' of the person you play is revealed chapter by chapter, making it fun to discover what happened to her, how she has grown up and how her life has changed. 

I've seen a lot of reviews commenting on the price in relation to the hours played to complete the game, but in my opinion you get what you pay for. Unpacking has so much to offer: you get to unpack, organise, decorate and fill new homes with memories while enjoying an amazing audio and visual experience. If you like this type of game, you will LOVE Unpacking!

I got this looking for something chill. And it is, for the most part—no stressful timers or loud noises or anything like that. But I was not expecting a game about putting things on shelves to be so emotionally impacting. It's a fantastic example of characterization through environment design; it puts you in the mind of the character as you try to fit the pieces of your life into each new situation, and you see how those pieces grow and change with her.

One level gave me mounting dread as I realized [spoiler]the protagonist's partner LITERALLY doesn't have space for her in his life[/spoiler], while another one made me legitimately excited that [spoiler]she finally had a living space that could fit all her clothes on hangers and all her books on bookshelves, with the diploma given pride of place on her office wall[/spoiler]. I know that doesn't sound like much, but contextually, with what it meant for the character, it was!

[h1] There's a lot to unpack here, pun intended. [/h1] 

Unpacking is a game whereby you (a unnamed female character) unpacks her boxes to her new room/house throughout different phases of her life.

[b] Pros: [/b]
- graphic and visual design 
- soundtrack
- helpful hints when things aren't where it's supposed to be
- the storyline, shown, not told
- secret achievements

[b] Cons: [/b]
- some stuff have strict places to be kept, not enough flexibility
- too short, lacks replayability
- price! 

[b] Should you get it? Yes (but only when it's on sale) [/b]

Full review with spoilers: 

So I found myself playing the game in a single 2 hour playthrough from start to finish, and with just 8 houses (levels) it's quite short for me, though the possibilities are nearly endless at where you keep certain items. I found myself enjoying the "storyline" most where the character's life is shown, not explicitly told, as she moves from her parents' home to a co-living with her art campusmates, to moving in with her boyfriend and then moving back to her parents' home when they broke up (tragic!), and then taking off to her own house and finally settling in a two-storey home with a baby on the way. The "breakup" level is cleverly shown - at first I was confused why the character was back at her old childhood room, until I realised the photo of her boyfriend and herself on the corkboard was marked as "invalid placement" by the red outline. On closer inspection it's revealed that she pinned over her boyfriend's face - and that's where the player understands with an "ahhh" moment. In addition, clever secret achievements are hidden throughout each level and the whole game itself, such as putting the toaster in the bathtub and flushing every toilet throughout all levels. 

However Unpacking isn't a "place-anywhere" type of game, where some items like electrical appliances must be placed near a power socket. For me at home, I keep my unused toaster unplugged and in a cabinet, but that isn't allowed in the game so it takes a while to get used to where the game restricts some item placement. That said, a helpful hint whereby a flashing red outline is shown on the item when things aren't where they are supposed to be, though this wasn't shown on the first level (I placed the boombox under the table and couldn't proceed to the next level, so I restarted it and had to do the level again).

As others have mentioned, 8 levels is pretty short for its price of $20, and it feels excessive. The Steam sale price of $14.80 should have been the actual price of the game - hence it's only worth to get when the game is on a promotion. It lacks replayability too, as the same levels present itself when you finish the game. I completed it in over 2 hours, hence it's no longer valid for refund and I can only repeat the same thing over again.

Unpacking（荷解き）がテーマのゲームです。
やることは引っ越しに伴う荷物の荷解きのみ。
ダンボールに入っている荷物を自分の好きな場所に好きなように置いていきましょう。

最初はストーリーのない単なるパズルゲームと思ってプレイしていきましたが、[b][u]ステージが進むことで「これら荷解きは同一人物の引っ越しに伴うもの」ということに気付かされます。[/u][/b]

住む場所（ステージ）や荷物の中身などで引っ越しに至る背景などが想像できるようになります。

考えてみれば引っ越しの多くは進学、転勤、結婚などの人生の分岐点や転機を迎えることで起きることです。
時には新たな生活に胸踊らせながら引っ越しをすることもあるでしょう。
時には辛いことが起きたことで引っ越しをすることもあるでしょう。
ゲームとして操作する内容は荷解きして配置していくだけでしかないのに、そういった引っ越しとその人生の変化を感じさせてくれるゲームです。

ちなみに
『台所に搬入した箱から衣類が出てくる（逆に寝室の箱からフライパンが出てくる）』
『収納場所の空きがなく持ってきた荷物の収納に頭を悩ませる』
といった、[b]引っ越しあるある（？）[/b]なシチュエーションもあります（笑）

Unpacking is a game that proves you don’t need dialogue, visible characters, or complex interactions to tell a deeply engaging story.  From the moment you start, you’re only narrative comes from the items you unpack, and yet it’s more than enough to stir a range of emotions, including a surprising amount of animosity towards a character you never see or speak to.

I would say that the game has a level of simplicity to it that makes it so easy to pick up and put down but also the emotions it evokes as you unpack someone’s life, one box at a time makes it very special.  I have played this whenever I am starting to feel my depression creep up on me and it's been helpful to play multiple times.  Something about myself having no connection to start with any of the items, I can feel the beloved childhood toy, a worn pair of shoes, or something that doesn’t quite fit with the rest, while the story unfolds without a single word, and yet you find yourself piecing together the life of the person you’re unpacking for, understanding their joys, sorrows, and struggles through the belongings they carry with them from place to place.

Whether you’re meticulously organizing every item to create a cozy, harmonious space, or embracing chaos within the game’s limits, there’s a satisfying freedom in how you approach each room.  I think it has a perfect blend of calming gameplay and subtle storytelling, offering a peaceful yet engaging experience that allows you to stay present and mindful of your surroundings.

Unpacking on Steam is a beautifully crafted and thought-provoking indie puzzle game that centers around the simple yet profound act of unpacking boxes and organizing belongings. At first glance, it might seem unassuming—a minimalist, pixel-art game that appears to focus solely on tidying up spaces—but as players progress through the game, it reveals itself as a nuanced narrative about life, change, and personal growth. The game’s art style is charming and understated, with soft colors and clean, simple visuals that evoke a sense of calm and reflection, perfectly matching its meditative gameplay style. The absence of dialogue and overt storytelling directs players to interpret the game’s narrative through the objects they unpack, making each player's experience uniquely personal and emotionally resonant.

Gameplay in Unpacking is surprisingly deep despite its straightforward mechanics. Players are tasked with placing items into various rooms across different stages of life—moving into a new home, growing up, changing jobs, and experiencing major life events. The game subtly guides players in arranging belongings in ways that reflect the character’s evolving personality, lifestyle, and circumstances. There is no time limit or explicit instructions; instead, players are encouraged to think about the significance of each item and its placement, fostering a sense of intimacy with the protagonist’s story. As the game progresses through different chapters, the items and room layouts tell a story of personal development, relationships, and transitions, often resonating emotionally with players who see their own experiences reflected in the mundane yet meaningful objects.

What makes Unpacking particularly compelling is its ability to convey complex emotional states through simple gameplay. Items like childhood toys, school supplies, photographs, and personal mementos serve as visual markers of memories, milestones, and emotional states. The game subtly explores themes such as nostalgia, longing, independence, and even loss, without ever explicitly stating them. This narrative depth, conveyed solely through the act of unpacking and organizing, transforms what might seem like a trivial task into a powerful storytelling device. The game’s pacing is gentle, allowing players to absorb each phase of the protagonist's life, creating a contemplative atmosphere that encourages reflection on one’s own personal journey.

The sound design and music further enhance the game’s introspective mood. The soundtrack features soft, ambient melodies that complement the minimalist visuals and slow pacing, fostering a tranquil environment. The sounds of objects being placed, drawers closing, and boxes settling create a satisfying tactile experience that immerses players in the act of organization. The lack of spoken dialogue or narration means that the game relies heavily on visual storytelling, which it executes masterfully. The subtle cues and visual storytelling invite players to interpret the narrative in their own way, making each playthrough a personal journey. The game’s ending is open to interpretation, leaving players with a lingering sense of reflection on the passage of time and the impermanence of life’s milestones.

Overall, Unpacking is a quietly powerful game that elevates a simple task into a meaningful exploration of human experience. Its minimalist design, emotional depth, and evocative storytelling make it a standout in the indie puzzle genre. It’s a game that rewards patience and introspection, offering a calming yet emotionally charged experience that stays with players long after they finish. Whether viewed as a nostalgic reflection on life’s transitions or as an artistic meditation on personal growth, Unpacking succeeds in turning an everyday activity into a profound narrative journey, demonstrating that sometimes the most ordinary actions can hold the deepest significance.

This is an absolutely cute little game for people with an organization itch. It is completely and utterly stress free,  It tells a story through a handful of stages. TLDR: game good but price is not proportional to current content amount + high likelihood of not getting any future content - especially when compared to other 2d pixel simulation games. 

Things I liked about the game : 
relaxing, puzzle-style game which can relate to real life. There's something inherently satisfying about putting away all the items from the boxes, arranging them in an aesthetic way, and designing a place which the character can call "home". The storyline explores how the items an individual owns, the way that their home is kept, reflect on the personality and life of an individual. In a way, the method of story telling is similar to game like house flipper, where you KNOW something is up, but it's up to you to deduce what has happened and piece together the story by yourself! 
Music is nice, wouldn't say that it's earth-shatteringly amazing. It's soothing yes, but other than that (imo) it doesn't stand out all that much against other games with similar lo-fi chill vibes kinda music. 

Reason why this is a thumbs down:
I think if you scroll through the comments, you will likely see alot of people commenting on the price of the game and how it's not the most "worth" it. Personally, I payed RM31 (GBP5.5) when I got this game on sale, because that's how much the steam store in my country was charging for it. 
For comparison, Stardew valley when not on sale is RM31, Terraria is RM23. Why do I bring these games up? Mainly because they are 2d,pixel simulatation-type indie games.  
For both, there was/is continued updates after release with free content that expanded on the base game, and both of these games can easily give you hundreds of hours of gameplay. 
On the other hand, this game (for a slightly higher price) has an average runtime of 2-8 hours, depending on how meticulous you are at organizing everything i suppose. Personally, my first run without hurrying was ~4 hours with 60% of achievements. 
While you might say that it's unfair to compare these games since they are different genres etc. etc. I think it's important to point out that the standard of games at this point in time is high, so games with limited content, without plans of future updates, and also are priced relatively high compared to other similar games, will definitely be at a disadvantage. 
So yeah, if you're planning on getting this game, maybe wait a few years to when it's 50% off or something.. if you're lucky there might even be additional content.

Do you enjoy organizing other people’s junk?
Do you have competitive OCD?
If the answer is yes to either of these, congratulations! Unpacking is GOTY baby! Ten out of ten! Every award! Move over, It Take’s Two! Review over.

If the answer is no... 
Congratulations! You just saved yourself a few annoying hours because Unpacking is the part of moving house that everyone resents in real life—except without the pizza, friends, or any of your own stuff. It’s a game that bravely asks the questions other developers are too afraid to ask like:
“Where does this mug go?”
“How about this cushion?”
“What about this pig mascot plush I’ve been carrying through five different apartments because apparently emotional attachment is stronger than common sense?”
And the best part? It’s the same items at every location plus a few more! Art imitating life! The accumulation of junk as you get older and refusing to throw any of it away.

Now for the gameplay. (It’s a short section). 
Drag object from Box A to Surface B until the game nods in approval. The placement rules don’t matter… except when they do. Book? Anywhere. Controller? Sure. Mug? Living room? Why not. Coffee pot? Counter only. Do not put it in the cabinet. Walkie-talkies? Closet drawer of course. Clothing basket? Keep guessing.

And what about the story? 
It’s all visual, which is kinda neat, but it landed somewhere between heartfelt indie storytelling and “I’m 14 and this is deep.”
“Oh, she went to college.”
“Oh, she moved in with a guy.”
“Oh, he sucks.”
“Oh, now she’s living alone.”
“Oh, now she’s in an LGBTQ+ relationship, and that probably should’ve been tagged.”
I’m sure it’s all very touching, but halfway through I stopped following her emotional journey and started speedrunning the task.

Final verdict: I don’t know what I was expecting, but this isn’t it. People own way too much stuff, and I apparently don’t enjoy organizing it for them. The only thing missing was someone asking me to help carry a couch up three flights of stairs, but that actually might have been more interesting.

Unpacking in Unpacking allows you to place anything, anywhere, so long as it fits in its place. This isn't a problem until everything is unpacked, and the game highlights what is "out of place." The only issue this creates is that it is never apparent where some things are meant to go outside of your own intuition as a player. You unpack the room based on where you, the player, would want to put things, but if it's not the piece of furniture the *game* wants something to be in, there's a small to large amount of redecorating that needs to be done depending on how "incorrectly" you unpacked the room. This isn't *that big* of an annoyance, but can definitely be an upset in the later levels where you're responsible for unpacking multiple rooms, sometimes with items intentionally being in the incorrect box for where they're intended.

That being said, Unpacking is a very relaxing and humble experience. Its design is intentional and quaint, and while some will say to wait for a sale, with the amount of pixel art and sound design done for the game, I'd say give it the full $20 if you can.

Unpacking is a relaxing game about unpacking boxes and arranging the items in their owner’s new home.  

The standout feature of the game for me was the environmental storytelling.  The items that are brought or not brought to each new house tell us something about this person’s life.  If you play with the mild puzzle elements turned on, the placement of the objects can convey something of their living arrangements.  I didn’t use the accessibility options myself, but I did appreciate they were there, especially if you want to go back and arrange the rooms how [i]you[/i] would want them to be.  The sounds used when clicking everything in place add to the very satisfying organisational experience.

The pixel art aesthetic is very pleasing to look at, and the objects are appropriately detailed and identifiable to avoid confusion.  In the case of books, for example, there is a level of visual co-ordination to show which books belong to a set, and if inclined you can group them together. Each item feels highly considered and contributes to the notion that these items belong to a real person, rather than blank default items. 

For a short game like this, there are some fun achievements involved, each one with a sticker reward in-game.  The sticker names give clues as to what interaction may trigger the achievement, though I think finding them by accident and figuring out what to do can be equally appealing.   Unfortunately, outside of this, the game may not offer a lot of replay value.  I could justify the price for myself, I think the game is well-crafted and an enjoyable experience, however as a direct cost/hours of game play, this is definitely on the pricier side.   I finished the game in about 4 hours. 

I recommend this game for a chill, slow-paced organisational experience, the opposite of actually moving house.

Unpacking — это та игра, которую я могу советовать всем, кто хочет отдохнуть и ничего не взрывать.

На первый взгляд — просто раскладывай вещи по местам. Но на деле это такой уютный и глубокий процесс. Больше всего мне нравится, что есть масса вариаций: вещи не привязаны к одному строгому месту, можно экспериментировать, и каждая комната у каждого игрока получается уникальной. Можно разложить всё идеально ровно, а можно чуть хаотично — и оба варианта правильные.

Это невероятно расслабляет. Включаешь игру, тихую музыку, начинаешь перебирать вещи персонажа, и будто сам выдыхаешь. Никаких таймеров, ошибок и стресса — только порядок (или творческий беспорядок, если захочется).

My first playthrough, with me taking my time to savor it, took about three and a half hours. I played through it twice the first day I got it and that experience took a total of about six hours. I put this at the top so people that really care about that kind of thing enough to choose to skip a gem like this because of it, can get that information. 

The value of a game is different to different people, though. There has been a lot said about this game's length, to the detriment of everything else that is contained within it, and that's tragic. 

This game is a journey. Not just through time, but through a person's life: through their joys, their sadness, their triumphs. And it's phenomenal, honestly. This game is one of the best I've ever seen at telling stories through the environment. I mean, it should be, since it's all about the environment. 

The things we carry through our lives, the objects we take with us, the items we absorb from others, and the things we tend to along the way tell volumes about us. For a non-spoiler example (and yes, absolutely, this game has spoilers to it): the stuffed pig toy that the main character brings with her through the entire game. When she's young, it's new(er): It's clean and soft and well-loved. As she ages and goes through different stages of her life, it ages, too. It gets discolored. Something tears it at some point. But then, later, someone tends to it. Very lovingly, too. The pig is cleaned, mended, and given a new bow around its neck. We can speculate on who and why. Was it the main character? or someone else?

Some spoiler examples of just absolutely phenomenal environmental storytelling: 

[spoiler] When she moves in with her boyfriend downtown. That relationship is doomed. It's obvious it is. He makes no room for her. She has to clear her own space. She (you) can move some objects around, but not others. If you want space for your underwear, you have to organize HIS stuff to make space, even though there's plenty of room. He clearly expands to fill all available space. 

The realities of their time together hang heavy in the air: she probably was expected to clean up; to minimize herself; to literally put her dreams away, as there's no room for any of her pursuits. You can't move any of his pictures on the wall, so there's no room anywhere for her accomplishments: her diploma can fit under the bed, though. 

It hurt my heart to unpack there, to so clearly see where that relationship would go, assuming she eventually chose to grow, instead of continuing to limit herself, to shrink herself to fit in his space -- the space he made unwelcoming to her. Even the shared home before their relationship had space made for her. A house with multiple people present. 

And, following the resolution to that doomed relationship, I perked up at the tiniest hint of what was to come, in her sock drawer of all places. [/spoiler]

Okay, enough spoilers.

Just, I cannot stress enough the quiet joy in this game. The creators of this game really nailed it in terms of tone, storytelling, and, honestly, hope. The sound design and music is phenomenal as well. The different tracks pair so well with the vibe of each stage. And, of course, the art style is just so good. The pixel art is crisp and clear. Again, you can pick up so many details in the art and so much care was given to this as well. I love that you can tell what ingredients in the kitchen were what: the appearance of the shichimi togarashi and mirin, especially. Just, SO GOOD.

Do I wish it was longer? Sure, that could be good, too. 

In a perfect world, where games didn't take massive amounts of time and often money as well, maybe there could be different "albums" where you got to play through different people's lives. That could be great. I know this studio would absolutely smash that out of the park, too. But I'm glad we live in a world where this game exists at all. And part of why I'm okay purchasing and keeping it, is because I want this group to thrive, to continue to create games, whether they're in this vein or not.  

I can't wait to see what they do next. And, to the developers directly: You all did such a great job. I am so pleased with this. And, with a bunch of LGBT+ friends in-flux at the moment especially, this game is a gift of joy and hope and it is deeply appreciated that it exists. Thank you so much.

Unpacking is a puzzle game about unpacking boxes and placing things logically.

The game is very well made and while there are no set story, you can interpret your own. The music is super relaxing and while it's not super creative, each tracks are good. The art style is super cute and there are a great variety of items and furniture, even if I think some of the items are re-used way too much. I would say a solid 25% of the items are re-used over each levels.

I love how the game is quite lenient on where you can place objects, but while it allows you for quite some freedom, I think some of the items could have more valid spots. I don't see why some stuffed animals can be set on the ground while some of them can't. Also why can you not keep a mug on your table, etc. The furniture could've also been slightly bigger, as the biggest areas to store pans and pots barely holds 2 of them. I could have done a much neater job if the storage was made slightly bigger, but without trying super hard to make everything tidy it did look rather messy once I finished the level. I couldn't make out some of the items due to the pixel art style, so that's also something to note.

The game is also definitely way too short for the listed price! $20 for 3.2 hours of gameplay is not worth it for any games ever. Yes the game is relaxing, wholesome and well polished, but there's no replayability once it's over... unless you want to re-reorganize everything over and over...

Overall, worth to get on sale because it is very short. Do note that it's a puzzle game despite it's appearance, as the items have only a few valid spots!

I absolutely loved this game. The art style is great and the storytelling is amazing. There's no spoken plot, but you can work out the protagonist's life through all the little details of their different homes.

It's a relaxing game to play but there's actually some level of difficulty. Trying to get everything packed away in the limited space is a challenge. You think you're done squeezing everything into the kitchen and then whoops, turns out there's some cups and plates in the box in the bedroom. Better rethink your organisation.

There are only two downsides: one (as a lot of reviewers have mentioned) is the length of the game. I thought I was taking my time but I still finished it in only 3 hours. I would love to see more content; there's huge potential for a whole new life story.

The other downside is that the game is quite restrictive at times. It won't let you progress if you've put items in the "wrong" place. I understand that I can't just dump everything on the floor or put a saucepan in the bathroom, but why do I HAVE to put my eraser on the desk instead of the shelf next to it? Why do my bathroom scales HAVE to be placed against a certain wall? The game doesn't indicate where some items should go, so it's just a case of moving things to different places until the game is happy with it and lets you move on.

Overall I really do like this game and I definitely recommend it. Perhaps wait until it's on sale though.

Interesting little puzzle game.  Its short. SUPER short.  5 hours and i 100% the game.  That's the biggest weakness here, the length of the game vs the price.  

Don't get me wrong, it was a funny little journey, and the game play was solid.  

The story i'm sure checks the right boxes for some people.  It is told mostly through the items you unpack and where they can go, as well as the captions on pictures when you finish the level.  Its an interesting narrative style, and you could, if so inclined, spend hours thinking about the little details in it.  As a stay-at-home dad home schooling his kid, i beat the game while the kid did their home work, and a couple of times through out the day i found my thoughts drifting to the game and the various little things that tug at the mind.  

The pixel art is fantastic.  I've come to loath fancy 3D graphics (which is a bit funny, as I stare at a 4k monitor), which so often are used to mask a weak or broken game.  Unpacking's PIxel art is beautiful yet simple.  you can easily identify most items at first glance. The only one that threw me was the koala magnet when i first unboxed it, it wasn't until i put it on the fridge that i was like, "Oh, its a Koala!"

All in all, the game is a fun way to spend a few hours.  Whether the price is right for you, is another matter entirely.

I'd like to end with a bit of a thought.  The narrative style, Game play mechanic, and art all deserve more time.  Further, i think they deserve multiple stories.  While i may usually decry diversity for the sake of diversity, in this sort of game, a diverse set of stories being told in the style would be fun.  We have this tale, of growing up and finding oneself. Why not a tale about a person growing old? one about a military family having to move every few years.  Or follow a kid from childhood through school, seeing how their personality changes as they face those challenges.  There is so much potential with this style of game.  I'd love to see the developers expand on it with more stories and characters.

But even if they don't, it was still a good tale. I'd recommend it to anyone that likes puzzles, wants a story that they have to figure out the details of, or wants a relaxing no-pressure game to spend some time on.

Let me begin by stating that I have had my eye on this game for a while now, and once it went on Sale, I could not resist anymore and bought it for about $15.00. 

The game is exactly what it advertises. It's a nice little Zen puzzle game that allows you to exercise your interior decorating sensibilities, while providing some nostalgia and sentimental flair. 

However, I have to agree with a lot of other reviews regarding it's length and price. The entirety of the game can be explored in a few hours if you're impatient, and there's not much replay incentive afterward. 

The game could be improved with a little more clarity and depth. There are a couple objects can be hard to distinguish upon first sight (maybe just have some labels or a brief description?), and the achievements could come with some hints rather than being totally random discoveries. The camera controls could be a little more refined. 

And of course, there should be more content overall at this price point, or some promise of expansion. Add some more secrets/achievements, enhance the "plot" a little bit and the complexity of the environment and how objects interact with one another, idk... The game has a really fun and simple mechanic, but feels too empty once everything's put away.

Unpacking is a casual game where you unpack boxes and put items from them into rooms in houses. It is a very basic puzzle game, insofar that you have to put the items in logical places and make sure they all fit in there, but the game is pretty much trivial in terms of difficulty – if you complete unpacking a house and have items in the wrong places, the game will tell you which items are in the wrong places, and you can easily just move them around and put them in the right places. You start out with one room, but some of the later levels have far more than that, with the final level being an entire, full-sized house.

The game is very simplistic, and almost all of the satisfaction you’ll get out of it is from this act of unpacking the boxes and seeing what the person has with them at this chapter in their life.

The game uses environmental storytelling to tell a story, about a child who grows up to be an adult and starts their own life. Each chapter in the game represents a significant change in their life, and as you go through, you learn the person’s interests, as well as see what they’re going through at that point in their life.

It’s fairly cute, and well-done, but it isn’t really enough if you aren’t into the core gameplay of unpacking and arranging things – and honestly, it’s not that interesting of a core mechanic, as it is very simplistic and it is mostly just kind of mindless and a little bit tedious.

Fortunately, the game is quite short (less than 5 hours long to 100%), so you won’t be stuck playing it for overly long.

All in all, it’s hard to recommend this game; it is kind of mediocre, and the clever environmental storytelling isn’t worth unpacking all eight levels of the game.

Unpacking é a definição perfeita de um Cozy Game. É uma experiência super relaxante e acolhedora em um jogo indie onde você organiza cômodos enquanto acompanha uma história cheia de significado, contada de forma bem sutil.

Tudo começa no [spoiler]quarto de infância da protagonista e, a cada fase, você vai ajudando ela a arrumar as coisas nas novas casas onde vai morar ao longo da vida. O mais legal é que, mesmo sem falas ou textos explicando tudo, o jogo transmite a história através de pequenos detalhes — como certos objetos que só podem ser colocados em lugares específicos. Essas escolhas simples acabam dizendo muito sobre os sentimentos da personagem e o momento que ela está vivendo.[/spoiler] 

É um jogo tranquilo, sem pressa, que respeita o seu ritmo. E, mesmo sendo simples, ele consegue te tocar de um jeito inesperado, deixando aquela sensação boa que fica com você depois de jogar.
Es ist einfach ein hübsches Spiel das eine nette kleine Geschichte erzählt.

Unpacking é um jogo incrivelmente único e cativante. A premissa de desempacotar caixas e organizar itens em diferentes fases da vida de uma pessoa pode parecer simples à primeira vista, mas o jogo consegue transformar essa rotina em uma narrativa profunda e emocional.
A atenção aos detalhes é impressionante. Cada objeto conta uma história, e a forma como eles se encaixam (ou não) nos espaços disponíveis faz você refletir sobre a vida e as mudanças que todos passamos. A trilha sonora é calma e combina perfeitamente com o ritmo relaxante do jogo.
Além disso, a falta de diálogos escritos ou falados não impede que o jogo transmita uma narrativa poderosa. Através dos objetos e dos espaços, Unpacking consegue comunicar sentimentos de crescimento, perda, amor e autodescoberta de uma maneira que poucos jogos conseguem.
Recomendo este jogo para quem procura uma experiência calma, mas emocionalmente recompensadora. É perfeito para relaxar após um dia cansativo ou para refletir sobre as pequenas coisas que fazem parte da nossa vida.

Nota: ★★★★★

[b]Rating:[/b] ★★★★ - Great
[b]Time Played:[/b] 4.5 hours

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
• Puzzle-like organization mechanic that’s both therapeutic and addictive
• Each level feels natural, gradually increasing complexity without feeling overwhelming
• Freedom to arrange items in various ways
• Satisfying sense of accomplishment when you complete a room
• In experimentation, put things in the right place\order to collect stickers\achievements (optional)
	
[b]Story\Dialogue:[/b]
• Quiet narrative revealed through environmental rather than direct storytelling
• Each move to a new home subtly conveys life changes and emotional development
• No dialogue, but the environment effectively tells a personal story of a Jewish lady from 11 years old to 32
	
[b]Graphics\Music:[/b]
• Charming pixel-art visuals that lend a cozy, nostalgic atmosphere
• Subtle sound effects make unpacking boxes and placing, moving and shaking items feel tactile
• Soothing background music that never distracts and relaxes the mood
	
[b]Before you Play:[/b]
• Ideal for players who appreciate low-pressure, meditative puzzle experiences and have a keen eye for environmental storytelling
• Completing it in a single session, it finished just before becoming repetitive
• Some items have one or two “correct” spots to progress and will highlight red near the end of the unpacking if it's in the wrong place
• The OCD will not be able to find perfect placements for everything and may need to sacrifice  symmetry for homeliness

Unpacking, for me, highlights the importance of not only having space for everything, but having *A* space for everything. It is a tiny luxury. Unpacking made me realize that what we own, as well as where we put it, does a significant part in terms of defining who we are. 

The gameplay of unpacking is contemplative. This isn't strictly like unpacking in real life, since you don't really know about an object - you simply know what it looks like. If we were unpacking, we may put things we use most often close to us, and things that we never use we may stow away. This is both freeing (you can group similar looking items together with no regard for their use) and troubling (if you run out of space, you can't just stow some items away knowing they won't be used). Overall this isn't too much of an issue, but it does come up here and there.

I think the most fascinating part of Unpacking is the idiosyncrasies it reveals about being a human, living in a space - both for yourself or for humans in general. Bug spray goes under the sink. Can opener goes with the silverware.  

This meditative exercise is given a nice sountrack, but I found I preferred the ambient sound effects. The developers have done an astounding job capturing a quiet stillness. Lone mourning dove calls. The gentle thrum of traffic. Gentle rain on glass. That's a haiku for you. Even the sound shaking of pill bottles is velocity dependent. It's evident great care was put into this game, and it's much appreciated.

I absolutely adored this game. It's got a simple concept: going through cardboard boxes and unpacking their contents where they belong in the main character's new living space. It reminded me a lot of Gone Home, in that you're learning all about people's lives by digging through their belongings, without ever actually meeting the people in question. There is zero text or dialog. Without spoilers, there are some plot twists that are delivered just by where exactly the game will let you place certain objects.

All in all, very soothing, and totally worth buying. I beat it in just under 3 hours, so the game doesn't overstay its welcome.

Honestly, I found this game more boring than relaxing, and somewhat chore-like. You can play how you want to a certain extent, but it does make you follow the in-game rules. I was absolutely floored that Australian "people" just leave their dirty ass Vans on the carpeted floor in their bedroom closet but the game does not allow me to put it on a shoe rack like a proper civilized person.

[h1]Я пережил что-то необычное...[/h1]

Еще с момента показа первого трейлера на какой-то выставке в году так 2020. Я понял что это тот проект в который я хочу поиграть. 
Спустя несколько лет я тут, готов в полной мере насладится всеми радостями и печалями переезда. Но я знаю что для многих современников проблема переезда просто не знакома, и я провел просто *как мне показалось, отличную аналогию* с переустановкой винды или покупкой нового компа.
Многие из нас могли долгое время оседать за одной системой, копить нужные файлы и воспоминания о людях, животных и вещах на своих жестких дисках.
Но рано или поздно приходит момент когда старому электронному другу нужно уйти на отдых, а вам жизненно необходимо обновиться до более новой и мощной машины.
Это заставляет нас перекопать все папки и схроны на дисках, для кого-то это коллекция модов на майкрафт, кто мог собирать нюдсы бывших, кто-то банально копил мемы для важных переговоров, а другой жадно скачивал всю музыку, я вот коплю все свои видео и фото проекты, все эффекты и пресеты, луты и фильтры, с недавнего времени сюда прибавилась коллекция ПнП настольных игр и журналов Мира Фантастики, Игромании. У каждого свой хлам, нужны он или не нужный знает только сам владелец, но это отлично передает ту самую атмосферу переезда!
Вы забираете все что можете с собой в коробки, а от остального, избавляетесь. И уже после переезда на новую систему, вы снова распределяете каждый ярлычок на рабочем столе, каждую папку на диске и настраиваете каждый элемент винды под себя. Великолепное чувство, если это делается по вашему желанию. Думаю хватит предисловий, давайте об игре...

[b][u]СЮЖЕТ/ЛОР[/u][/b]
Сюжет... Нет, я бы лучше сказал, история! В игре нет событий которые проведут вас за ручку через все потрясения главной героини. Здесь есть только последствия которые вы можете наблюдать посредством переезда. И все начинаете безобидно, как любому нормальному ребенку родители не навязывают стереотипы, у неё есть как и футбольный мяч, так и гора плюшевых игрушек, как и детские книжки, так и комиксы. Уже сейчас можно понять что человек может вырасти в разностороннюю личность и ему будет куда проще определится в жизни. Переехав, вы замечаете еще более обширную часть новых вещей которые теперь преследуют героиню, это и пубертат(прокладки), и депрессия(плеер под подушкой), и не умение отпускать(старые игрушки или плакаты).
Переехав еще пару раз, пережив неприятные события, вы заметите как многие детские или подростковые проблемы все еще перебираются вместе с ней на новое место жительства, так в одной из коробок обнаружится фото с бывшим парнем, зачем его было брать с собой если это несет только боль, не понятно. Но так уж устроены мы, и многим все так же трудно отпускать но это пройдет со временем, и понимая это она смело прячет эту фотографию куда подальше.
Все что здесь описано не расскажут вам никакие описания предметов, или же записки в дневнике. Все это сможет понять лишь уже повзрослевшей человек, который проживал или видел как проживают подобное другие люди. Эта игра давит на одно из самых тяжелых чувств, чувство ностальгии.

[b][u]СТИЛЬ(ГРАФИКА/SOUND DESIGN)[/u][/b]
Пиксели преследуют нас на протяжении всей компьютерной эпопеи, и сколько градаций эволюции они пережили, будет трудно сосчитать без конкретных познаний в этой сфере.
Стиль пиксель арта выбранный в этой игре мне очень нравится, подход к каждому объекту просто невероятен. Я даже где-то слышал что для этой игры было записано около 10.000 разных звуков. Что уже автоматически заставило меня начать кидать кастрюли по всему дому, что бы послушать звук от каждой поверхности. И это я даже не аудиофил. Самое главное и любимое мною упоминание, абсолютно весь дизайн игры выполнен в одном ключе и дополняет друг друга, каждый элемент идеально вписывается в концепцию и не выделяется. Он не тянется к звездам, он телескоп дающих на них посмотреть. Разработчики взяли уже давно работающие элементы и просто, правильно их совместили. В купе с изометрическим пиксель артом и чудесным звуковым сопровождением вы получаете достойнейший проект!

[b][u]GAMEPLAY[/u][/b]
Если говорить просто, без всего что я выше описывал, для тупых так сказать. ДА, в этой игре вы просто раскладываете предметы. Здесь нет прокачки, разветвлений сюжета, кучи веток диалогов или других современных вещей. Но они здесь и не нужны, эта игра доберется до каждого, и придет в его жизнь тогда когда она ему будет нужна. Здесь всего от силы 2-4 часа игрового процесса, но этого ДОСТАТОЧНО. Это вам не симулятор переезда, это медитативный пазл-гейм, смотрите на теги в стиме. Каждый новый переезд не будет испытанием! Каждый новый переезд будет всего лишь расслабляющей расстановкой предметов, которым нужно своё место. Как и нам всем :D

Некоторым игра может показаться слишком короткой, но лучше раньше закончить чем поздно опомнится.

[b][u]Что в итоге?[/u][/b]
Я, кайфанул. После прохождения, мне не хотелось писать обзор ибо на душе был лишь дзен. Спасибо авторам, это было невероятно!

I personally would recommend waiting for a sale, as there is only 3-5 hours of gameplay depending on how methodical you are. Price tag aside though, this game is beautifully simple and the environmental storytelling is both heartwarming and heartbreaking. A few of my favorite moments were [spoiler](1) when the protag is moving in to their boyfriend's cluttered apartment and the only place to put their diploma is under the bed, (2) the next chapter, where we move back into our childhood bedroom and keep the photo of said boyfriend, but the only place you're allowed to put it is hidden away in a cabinet, and (3) the box in the last chapter that's just chock full of the same book over and over again. At first I thought this was just a lazy way to add lots of baby books since a nursery is added, until I realized the protag's hobby this whole time has been art and they finally made it as a children's book illustrator.[/spoiler] Also there's an achievement for putting the toaster in the bath tub so do with that what you will. Overall loved it and no game has made me so overwhelmed yet so at peace at the same time <3

Смешанные впечатления от игры на данном этапе...
С одной стороны, действительно это довольно залипательно и, как и говорят нам разработчики, медитативно. Музыка не отвлекает, довольно приятная. Ты проходишь каждый этап-уровень игры и видишь, как развивалась жизнь персонажа, подмечаешь этапы в жизни, какие-то забавные, какие-то даже немножко грустные, а на каком-то этапе и вовсе ностальгические. 
Порой бывают моменты, когда ты не знаешь, куда какой предмет поставить и что это такое. Тут не помешали бы редкие подсказки, либо уж пусть дадут позволение игрокам ставить всё туда, куда они хотят. 
Но в общем ощущения приятные. Если бы не одно "НО".


Увидев в меню три альбома, я была уверена, что это три разных персонажа с тремя разными историями. Однако оказалось, что нет. Это просто три места для разных сохранений, грубо говоря. Потому что персонаж один и жизнь одна. В какой-то момент предметы на уровнях тоже, в подавляющем большинстве, одни и те же. И это становится немного муторно, надоедает расставлять одни и те же предметы почти по одним и тем же местам. И не то, чтобы у тебя было много вариантов для смены остановки, так как некоторые объекты "привязаны" к определённым местам.

И вот на фоне всего этого, всего за один уровень с несколькими подуровнями-этапами жизни, нынешняя цена кажется завышенной. Не соглашусь с многими комментами ниже, ну не на 200р, но явно не на 400+. 

По итогу, думала, что контента будет больше, а оказалась немного разочарованной. Надеюсь, что со временем добавят ещё и желательно бесплатно, так как одного персонажа здесь явно мало.

Не могу сказать, советую я игру или нет... Если кого-то не пугает цена, то определённо да. Но если вы считаете, как и я, что одного персонажа с его историей в 5-7 уровней (честно, не помню точно сколько их, но не очень много, некоторые уровни маленькие), то, пожалуй, что нет. Либо подождите и понадейтесь на то, что контента добавят, либо пройдите мимо вовсе. 
Я бы рефанднула, но уже поздно...

Very relaxing to do the unpacking.  Also very interesting, subtle way to convey a story.  Speaking as someone who has had to move very often since turning 18 (over a decade, longest I've lived in 1 place was 3 years and moved more than 10 times), the things that stay with you over move after move are the things that really are the most important.  Those things do end up telling a story about you, your life, and your priorities.  Great idea for a game

A calm, intimate, and surprisingly emotional experience. There are no dialogues or battles, just boxes, objects, and empty rooms... but behind each move is a story more real than you'd expect.

What I enjoyed most is the almost real-life progression: watching someone grow, move through different stages of life, share spaces, or gain independence as their situation and surroundings improve. Each new home tells its own story without a single word, and little by little, you begin to understand who you’re unpacking for.

It’s not a game you need to replay, but one that sticks with you for how it tells its story. And if you’ve ever moved, you’ll probably find yourself placing things in the “right” spot without even realizing why.

By the way, I still don’t know which drawer the duck goes in.

子供の頃から大事にしていたぬいぐるみ。
数の増えていく本やボードゲーム。

[h1][b]一つ一つに想いが宿る[/b][/h1]

人の生活の軸となる[b]衣・食・住[/b]。
それらは、人生を映し出す鏡。

これは、そのうちの一つの[b]『住』[/b]
[b]『持ち物』に焦点をあてたゲーム[/b]。

ゲームの流れとしては、
ダンボールに梱包されていた荷物を
適した位置にアンパック（荷ほどき）するだけ。

全ての持ち物を適切な場所に置くと
ステージをクリアすることができる。


最初はパズルゲームかと思っていたけど
[b]ADVの方が近いな[/b]と遊んでて感じた。

ゲームのシステム自体は[b]ほぼ作業[/b]。
とてもじゃないが楽しいとは言えない。
少なくとも、これ単体で考えればだが。

移り変わるステージで、持ち物を並べていく。
[b]変わらない物、変わっていく物[/b]。

その繋がりから移り行く時代を感じ、
自ずとドラマ性が感じられることだろう。

結局のところ
これは、テキストの出ない[b]“読み物”[/b]なのだ。
（ステージクリア時などに最小限の説明はある）

もちろん、持ち物の並べ方一つ一つをこだわって
自分好みの部屋模様を作ってみるのもいい。

ゲームである以上、クリアのために
『この場所にこれを置いてはいけない』
という条件は用意されてはいるものの、
特定の物を特定の場所に置くことで解除される実績もある。

淡々とクリアを目標にしているプレイヤーからすると
作業ばかりで退屈な作品かもしれないが、
[b]端々から物語を感じたい[/b]という人にはオススメの作品。

I've only had this game for a few weeks, and I've already played it twice! It's very charming and pleasant, and I really love the art style. I like the story, and how it progresses through gameplay instead of cutscenes or dialogue. The vibes of the music, art, and direction are impressively clear in the storytelling without actually telling you explicitly what's going on. I think my favorite example of that is when she's moving in with her boyfriend and there's a really clear atmosphere of feeling unwelcome and like there's just not enough space to be yourself (degree under the bed, anyone?).

[h1] A delightfully zen puzzler that oozes charm and relaxation. Unpacking is a wonderful time and concept that unfortunately is quite short, leaving you wanting more [/h1]

Unpacking is a light puzzler that has you unpacking boxes in various rooms across eight levels that span roughly twenty years. Boxes may contain items for other rooms and items have a rough position they should be in within each room; fortunately the game will highlight out of place objects in red, giving you a clue that they need to be moved. 

There is a light story going on in the background as the individual whose items you are unpacking moves and grows through their life, adding a bit to the charm that is present. Aesthetically the game is wonderful to look at - I really dig this particular art style. The music is lovely to boot and has an ending song that I think will warm a lot of hearts. 

My only complaint is that the game is quite short for its price point and ends rather abruptly - I genuinely thought there would be more. 

If you enjoy puzzlers or are seeking something on the relaxing side, check this out when it hits its first sale.

[h1]Unpacking - Desembrulhando Memórias e Montando Lares com Poesia[/h1]

Introdução:
Em um cenário onde o caos das mudanças se entrelaça com a doçura das memórias, Unpacking emerge como uma jornada transcendental. Este jogo, mais do que uma mera experiência digital, é um convite poético para desdobrar lembranças e construir aconchegos em um novo lar. Meio quebra-cabeças, meio decoração de interiores, Unpacking sussurra a história de vidas desembrulhadas das caixas.

Desembalando a Experiência:
Unpacking transcende os limites do convencional, levando você a uma odisseia emocional. A mecânica única, semelhante a quebra-cabeças de blocos, desafia sua mente enquanto você organiza e reorganiza, transformando o ato mundano de desembalar em uma dança de descobertas e nostalgia. Cada item retirado das caixas é uma peça do quebra-cabeça da vida, uma história a ser contada.

Decoração de Interiores da Alma:
O jogo não é apenas sobre colocar móveis e objetos nos lugares certos; é sobre moldar o espaço com a essência daqueles que ocupam esse novo lar. Cada escolha de decoração, cada disposição, conta uma história mais profunda. A decoração torna-se uma linguagem silenciosa que fala sobre as experiências, paixões e conexões que estão se desdobrando diante de seus olhos.

Descobrindo Pistas Sutis:
Enquanto desembrulha lembranças, Unpacking oferece pistas delicadas sobre a vida que está emergindo das caixas. Uma fotografia antiga, um livro desgastado, cada objeto é um elo com o passado, uma janela para compreender a história por trás das mudanças. A narrativa se desenrola de maneira sutil, convidando-o a desvendar os mistérios dessa jornada íntima.

Recomendação:
Unpacking é mais do que um jogo; é uma poesia interativa que captura a beleza e a complexidade da experiência humana. Se você busca uma aventura que transcenda os limites da jogabilidade convencional, mergulhando profundamente na teia de emoções, Unpacking é uma escolha obrigatória. Suas mecânicas inovadoras, combinadas com uma narrativa que se desenrola como as páginas de um diário, transformam este jogo em uma obra-prima interativa. Prepare-se para se perder nas camadas profundas de significado enquanto desembrulha não apenas pertences, mas memórias e emoções. Unpacking é uma experiência que permanecerá contigo muito depois de ter guardado a última caixa.

Schön gezeichnetes Puzzlespiel, das leider recht schnell in Arbeit ausartet.

Dieses Spiel möchte uns die Freude und Erlebnisse bescheren, die man bei einem erfolgreichen Umzug erlebt, wenn es darum geht, die Kisten auszupacken. Und genau dieses Gefühl vermittelt das Spiel auch ziemlich gut. A game that is about taking things out of boxes and arranging them in rooms, which is the disguise of a story that is about the life of a person told through their possessions. Not only do the items themselves tell you about their journey through life, but the ways in which the environments are arranged - and more importantly, how they allow you to arrange your items in them - tell you a lot about how the person we're following fits in. The items you unpack and their relation to the space they have to fit into is used to subtle and great effect.

[spoiler]Without a doubt the most powerful example of this used in the game is the episode moving in with a boyfriend: the way everything's arranged means you have to move a LOT of stuff just to fit in making it feel like you're moving into a space that doesn't really want you there, but the most painful part by far is that your framed college degree, which usually takes pride of place on the wall, has to go UNDER THE BED as though it simply doesn't exist. Brutal.[/spoiler]

The artstyle is pretty cozy and is generally readable, although I did have trouble figuring out what one or two items were (which is important, because sometimes you'll get items that aren't meant for the room their box is in). The game does sometimes have seemingly illogical item placement rules, but you can turn them off in the options if it bothers you too much; I would recommend NOT turning them off for your first playthrough tho, just to get the intended experience which is important to the story.

Overall, a very comfy experience that allowed me to indulge my OCD tendencies wonderfully. No, seriously, it's absolutely vital that all the books of a certain thickness are arranged on that exact shelf in a specific order from tallest to shortest and I will brook NO arguments to the contrary.

I really wanted to like this game. I really, really did and was looking forward to it for a while.

And indeed, there's a lot to enjoy about it. The game is absolutely gorgeous, with absolutely beautiful artwork, just so many wonderful sprites, a great story almost entirely told by you putting the pieces together from context cues as you unpack, and see what's different, what's the same, etc, each you move, with a soundtrack that definitely compliments all those sentiments  to boot, resulting in a very comfy, relaxing, stress-free game that's just pouring charm and heart. 

And indeed, on top of that, there's a variety of great accessibility options, such as the ability to place items wherever you want if you're not particularly interested in the "puzzle" aspect of the game, and the game doesn't demean or punish your or anything for choosing that, which I definitely have to applaud the devs for. That's all wonderful and appreciated to say.

Unfortunately, despite that, while I'd like to say that would be enough for me to recommend it, and I really want to, I ultimately can't. 

That's in large part because, playing the game under normal options, it's meant to function as a "puzzle" game of sorts, where the are "right" and "wrong" locations for each objects (as they're correct locations are both meant to serve as the puzzle of the game and also serve as environmental story-telling as well, as just the simple fact of where you can or can't place certain items reveals a lot about the characters as the game progresses).

That's fine in theory, but the execution is lacking. First off, because while the pixelwork is beautiful, it's nonetheless not always clear what a specific item is supposed to be in the first place. And if you don't even know what an item is, even if you were to know what the puzzle would be otherwise, if you're not even sure what an item is, it's going to be hard to figure out how to play it (like, for instance, an item that's apparently actually a draw-erase board I easily mistook for something akin to a Wacom drawing tablet or THQ's uDraw tablet accessory, an easy mistake to make considering how many art items there are and whether tablet or dry-erase board, they're both art related, so yeah, that kinda thing can easily lead to confusion).

Having some kind of tool-tips when you select an item that says what it is would greatly help with this, because while most items are clearly identifiable due to the wonderful spritework, when you come to one of those few exceptions that just confuses you with what it even is, that's not a particularly fun experience.

Furthermore, playing the game normally, you're basically trying to figure out the "puzzle" of where the character you're playing as would have placed the item.

Only problem with that is, you're given no real hints. You just place items wherever you think makes sense, the items that are "wrong" will be highlighted with an outline, and while you will probably get a bulk of the items right without too much problem, for those that are wrong, you just have to move them around until you happen to stumble onto the "right" answer.

Which, as I mentioned earlier, is great for environmental storytelling and learning about the characters.

But it's absolutely terrible from a "puzzle" perspective, because there are no hints, no clues, no particular way you could possibly know what's right or wrong in any particular house as the whole point seems to be discovering the characters' lives and how they change as they age and grow, which is all well and good, but a puzzle game, at least in so far as this one is constructed, is a terrible way to get that across, because you just have to stumble onto the "answer." And while the answer itself might be satisfying, the process of figuring it out is just trial-and-error, which is very much fun and unsatisfying in a puzzle game. 

On a related note, playing the game normally, it also hits on another one of my pet peeves in video games: not being able to decide whether the player-character is an avatar for the player or if you're playing as and controlling an avatar representing yourself. 

In Unpacking's case, you're very clearly meant to be assuming to the role of a very defined character, if playing the game "normally." 

But then, if that's the case, why is one of the very first thing's you do be able to actually NAME the player character, as if it is you, with stuff thereafter referred to as "your room" and the like as a result. 

It's very clearly not my room at all! And I'm very clearly not playing as myself at all either! So why "pretend" like I am and allow the player to name themselves, instead of the MC just having their own defined name. Of course, not that that requires a specific name--the MC doesn't actually need to be given any particular name at all. I'm just confused why I'm given the option to choose the name of a character who's very much not me, as if they were. 

I dislike that in RPGs like Persona 4 and 5, and I dislike it hear. There's no reason to give the player the ability to select a name when they're not playing as themselves. It just results in a mixed-message that feels weird and confusing. 

Now, to go back to something else I mentioned that's directly related to my complaints: while playing the game "normally" you're meant to put objects in particular places and stuff, assuming the role of the game's main character.

However, the developers did indeed include an option to allow you to put items wherever you want as I mentioned earlier, and that's a greatly appreciated option, and if you choose it, while you lose the effects of the puzzles/environmental story-telling, as you're warned about when you pick that option, because you can put items wherever you want, the game gives you much more creative freedom in that mode and it truly feels more like you're actually unpacking and decorating your own homes, and thus justifying the choice to allow you to name the protagonist if you choose to enable that option.

The problem being, even if you enable that option, it's still obviously very much confined by the game being designed as a "puzzle" game first and foremost. 

As a result, even under that setting, you're still very much confined by stuff like the amount of hangers in the closet for actually hanging clothes, the amount of shelf/bookcase space in your bedroom for displaying stuff and similarly the amount of space on your desk as well, the amount of cupboards and storage in the kitchen, and so forth. It's kinda the exact opposite situation as playing the game normally, because playing it "normally," you don't have to worry about that type of thing TOO much because there are right and wrong answers for things regardless. 

However, if you choose to play with the "put stuff anywhere" option enabled, you're almost certainly come up with some great idea for how you want to decorate your house, but be limited by shelf/desk/cupboard space/just general real estate with no option for just getting new hangers or bookcases or shelves or anything and end up having to compromise anyway.

Which naturally makes perfect sense. Because the game is designed as a puzzle game first and foremost, and so it naturally follows that even under a "no rules" mode, you'd still be limited by that fact. Like, I can't really fault the devs for that and don't blame them for that or anything, as it's just what the game is, for better or worse, take it or leave it, and it's not like it's an inherent wrong choice or anything.

However, the result of all this is a game that just feels a bit "off" no matter what: either you're trying to solve the "puzzle" of the MC's life while masquerading as an avatar, or you try to do things your way, but are still constrained and restricted from doing what you truly what by the inherent nature of the game. 

A wonderful effort w/lots of love and soul put into it which I so desperately want to love, but this is not for me.

全成就了，很轻松惬意的收纳小游戏（前提是你没有强迫症），前面玩的时候真有点逼出强迫症，相比于这个，一大难点还是很多物品根本辨别不出到底是什么，经常会有这是什么这个为什么放这的疑问。上手难度很低，即使是没接触过的舍友也玩的很开心，比较解压的还是。
  除去玩法，隐藏的主线也是一大亮点，跟随主角来到一个又一个新家，打开一个又一个未知的行李，无论是新物品还是曾经的老物件都会给我带来一丝惊喜，并且拼凑出主角的人生。印象很深的就是主角婚后家居风格变成了清一色的灰黑风，和之前多彩个人风格强烈的房间完全不同，推测是男方的喜好，自己的证书也没地方挂起来了只能塞进床底，感慨挺深的。从一个小卧室，到两层楼的大别墅，主角从幼年进入大学，相爱，分手，养育后代，最后的谢幕看到主角一路的脚印，陪伴着主角走过这么长的路，还是很感人。
  流程5小时左右，全成就也比较简单，成就中有很多细节挺有意思的，极力推荐。
So, I did not expect a game about unpacking boxes to make me cry, but here we are...The amount of storytelling that they do in this with LITERALLY boxes of things is kinda wild. 10/10

Okay.. so pretty much this game is such a fast and easy finish. There are like 7 different years in the game which are full of 1-3 rooms (except for the last one with like 6 rooms) to decorate with the furniture items you unbox. All of this can literally be done in a short amount of time of 4 hours (or 6 like me). For a game that is originally listed for $20? I don't believe it is AT ALL worth that price.

I would understand if it was $5 in my opinion. For the amount of levels you get to decorate, that is a much more reasonable price. If the game was full of like 200-1000+ levels, then sure it would definitely be worth the $20 because there is more content to work with.
I think the developers should have expanded and built more on this game than what they released. They could have done much more to have more replayability and much more content to the game.

>> I'll give you an idea; you could have created a community tab kind of thing, where people can create and build their own rooms of any size they like. People could also be able to choose whether they want specified items to be part of the rooms that they created or not (for the community). This would have been MUCH better!! BETTER YET- this would have been like those room decorating flash games, from the old barbie and polly pocket days (if you know.. YOU KNOW what I mean).
You guys could still do the ideas I mentioned, and more people would be willing to buy this game for $20! However, even on its latest (and lowest price I've seen) sale its not worth the $13 price I paid. I don't regret it, I enjoyed the game and would look forward to more free updates that actually add WAYYYY more than what we received. Do you know how many games I have bought for $3 and they have wayy more content and playtime than this?

[i]Unpacking[/i] is one of the simplest things you'll ever play, but it's narratively deeper and more affecting than games with volumes of voiced dialogue and lore bibles.

More of us need to get this shining [b]gem[/b] into the hands of people that don't routinely play games, because it will broaden their definitions of what the medium is capable of.

Game Summary

Unpacking is an adorable, aesthetic, simple game where all you do is unpack boxes and organize the main character's belongings in any way you see fit. It is relaxing, calming, and peaceful, as long as you don't stress yourself out over placing the items.

My Personal Rating

Seeing as how I've played this game for over 9 hours as of 9.20.22, I am definitely in love with it! I haven't been able to stop myself from playing it over and over again. I have 4 save files currently, and I've just been very entertained with coming up with different layouts of the rooms. If I were to rate this game out of 10 I would give it a 10/10 based on the actual game play and how smooth the game runs, the overall story line, the audio and visuals, and the ability to keep someone with ADHD entertained for hours.

My Recommendation

I highly recommend Unpacking to anyone who is searching for a game to play that doesn't require much energy or attention. Also, this game is great for anyone who needs a bit of a break. The sound effects and music are also very lovely to listen to.

[h3] Positives [/h3]
The game is sweet and fun! I enjoyed the gameplay and music! The game is very charming, and I would recommend, but on sale! The reoccurring items, collectable stickers and discovering new spots is very fun. The levels progress nicely as you advance through the story. I found the story to be charming, although there isn't as much personalisation as the mc continues to grow up. 

[h3] Negatives [/h3]
However did I ran into a number of issues. First off, the game is very short. I bought it on sale for half the price so this was no issue for me, however I don't think I would buy it full price. The repeat level with new items was fun at first, but got confusing for me personally as some items from the previous level got moved and, or removed. As someone has already mentioned games gets more specific with each level in regards to certain items which doesn't always makes sense to me personally. It was fun at the start but was very bothersome at the last level. Like certain plants are not allowed on the floor for some reason? 

One wish that I feel might be more personal is that I see no point in naming the character at all. We don't get to participate or change the events, certain items are not allowed in certain rooms and there is no real way to make the game more you (apart from organizing items in a different manner).

Edit: Also minimal replayability. Even if you start another album its the same rooms, objects, etc. The lack of freedom in placing items really shows when you are replaying the game

I completed this in 3 hours- spread over two days, because i expected it to continue, so i kept playing.
I really wish that there was an option for free-play, because then it would be worth any dollar amount- but with how short-lived this was, this would be better off as a free-to-play game.

This review is coming from the perspective of someone who likes to keep things tidy in real life and organized in a very systematic, personalized way, so just keep that in mind as it's very important.

Obviously because of the type of person I am, this game immediately appealed to me. I started the first level and just started freely organizing it the way I wanted to. However, once I was done the game suddenly told me "yeah uhhh no - it has to be done *this* way." As someone who has a very rigid system for this, this just sucks! It meant that instead of enjoying organizing all the stuff, I had to play the game around how it wanted me to organize it, which meant putting a bunch of items on the floor at first because some of the places it wanted me to organize stuff in was just nonsensical to me, and so it very weirdly just turned into a draining experience I wanted to be over with by the time I was halfway through just the 3rd level.

And honestly, I don't think that would be very important if the point of the game wasn't to organize stuff. Yes I know that the game has that option to enable to make it not matter basically, but I saw that as the game basically admitting to itself that it sometimes asks you to organize things in spots that are just weird instead of an option because the game's "too hard". That's why I'm considering this whole thing as a genuinely massive con for this game. Since the main kinds of people this game would naturally appeal to be ones that enjoy having things organized, those are also the kinds of people that already have specific ways of going about it, so this just doesn't work.

Aside from that, the environmental storytelling is actually really really good, but since it's in the background with only exposition and not much to glean on stuff like character motivation and complex emotions and whatnot (even though we do get some of that here, but not a lot), I can't really consider this an outstanding narrative or anything like that, but it's pretty good and interesting.

Overall, this game's an easy 5.5/10 for me (so C-tier, which is to say it's ok). It's the only game where my sessions on it were so short and I had so many of them because I had to stop it prematurely each time from frustration on it not letting me organize the way I think is genuinely right (I am very strict on it in real life when making it a priority, as I said). I'm literally the target demographic for this game and didn't enjoy it.
